chapterTitle: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Impact of Different Lesions on Motor and Sensory Systems

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: In lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg) the lesion is in one of the following arteries:
questions.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) results from PICA infarction, causing ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ataxia, and hoarseness.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Chorea:
options: Is due to lesion in the substantia nigra.
May be due to lesion in the internal capsule.
Is associated with exaggerated tendon jerk.
Is associated with increased gamma activity
questions.explanation: Chorea is associated with hypotonia. Option C is correct. Chorea results from basal ganglia (caudate/putamen) lesions causing involuntary, irregular movements with reduced tone. Option A is wrong (substantia nigra lesions cause Parkinsonism, not chorea). Option B is wrong (internal capsule lesions cause UMN signs). Option D is wrong (exaggerated tendon jerk occurs in UMN lesions, not chorea). Option E is wrong (increased gamma activity causes hypertonia, opposite of chorea).
questions.keyConcept: Chorea presents with irregular, involuntary movements and hypotonia due to basal ganglia dysfunction.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The neurotransmitter used by the axons of substantia nigra neurons which project to the caudate and putamen is :
questions.explanation: The neurotransmitter used by substantia nigra neurons projecting to caudate and putamen is dopamine. Option C is correct. These neurons form the nigrostriatal pathway. When they degenerate (as in Parkinson's), dopamine levels in the striatum drop, causing motor symptoms. Option A is wrong (ACh is used locally in striatum). Options B, D, E are wrong neurotransmitters for this pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine is the nigrostriatal neurotransmitter; its deficiency causes Parkinson's disease motor symptoms.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following nuclei affected in hemiballismus?
questions.explanation: Hemiballismus is characterized by violent, flinging movements of contralateral limbs resulting from damage to the subthalamic nucleus, disrupting the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Hemiballismus: subthalamic nucleus lesion.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The main input of the basal ganglia is to:
questions.explanation: The caudate nucleus (with putamen forming the striatum) is the main input structure of the basal ganglia, receiving excitatory corticostriatal projections and sending output via the globus pallidus.
questions.keyConcept: Main basal ganglia input: caudate nucleus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Concerning the basal ganglia function, which is NOT true:
options: Caudate nucleus plan the sequence of patterns of movement.
Caudate nucleus modifies the timing of movements.
Putamen helps execution of subconscious learned pattern of movement.
Basal ganglia mainly increases the muscle tone.
questions.explanation: Basal ganglia mainly regulate/inhibit movement, not increase muscle tone. Option D is correct. The basal ganglia work through indirect pathways to inhibit excessive movement and regulate motor planning. Increased muscle tone is a brainstem/spinal cord function. Options A, B, C, and E all accurately describe basal ganglia functions in movement planning, timing, and suppression of unwanted movements.
questions.keyConcept: The basal ganglia modulate movement patterns and timing while suppressing involuntary movements, rather than directly increasing muscle tone.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Lesion of the internal capsule results in:
options: Spastic paralysis of the contralateral side of the body.
Flaccid paralysis of both sides of the body.
Clonus in muscles of the same side
Exaggerated tendon jerk on the same side of the lesion
questions.explanation: The internal capsule contains descending motor fibers that cross to the contralateral side. Lesions cause contralateral spastic paralysis (UMN signs) because the corticospinal tract has already crossed at the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule damage produces contralateral motor deficits because motor pathways cross rostrally at the pyramidal decussation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Arcuate nucleus is found in:
questions.explanation: The arcuate nucleus is found ventral to the pyramids in the medulla. It is a small nucleus that gives rise to some of the ventral external arcuate fibers that enter the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Arcuate nucleus found ventral to pyramids in medulla

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: What is the term for small infarcts in deep non-cortical white matter or the brainstem that result from the occlusion of penetrating branches of cerebral arteries?
questions.explanation: Lacunar infarcts are small deep infarcts in penetrating artery territories causing 'lacunes.' They result from lipohyalinosis of small penetrating arteries. These small vessel strokes affect basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule, pons. Option A is CORRECT. They differ from cortical infarcts (B) which affect the cortex. The answer is A. Lacunar strokes are associated with hypertension and diabetes.
questions.keyConcept: Lacunar infarcts are small, deep infarcts from lipohyalinosis of penetrating arteries - associated with hypertension.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a recess of the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The lateral recess is the only true recess of the fourth ventricle. It extends laterally beneath the superior cerebellar peduncle and opens at the foramen of Luschka into the subarachnoid space.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral recess is a recess of fourth ventricle

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 25‑year‑old woman presents with proximal, jerky, non‑purposeful movements of the limbs accompanied by hypotonia. Degeneration of which central nervous system structure is most likely responsible?
options: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Chorea (jerky, non-purposeful movements) with hypotonia results from caudate nucleus degeneration in Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant condition.
questions.keyConcept: Chorea pathophysiology

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Sections in lower level of pons show:
questions.explanation: Sections at the lower level of pons show the middle cerebellar peduncle (entering), vestibular nuclei (medial and inferior), and facial nerve nucleus. The superior cerebellar peduncle is at higher midbrain levels.
questions.keyConcept: Lower pons: middle cerebellar peduncle, medial and inferior vestibular nuclei

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Superior cerebellar decussation:
options: Present in inferior level of midbrain.
Its fibers descend in all segments of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar decussation (decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles) is present at the inferior level of the midbrain. Tectospinal tract decussates at the midbrain but is not the superior cerebellar decussation.
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar decussation at inferior midbrain level (superior cerebellar peduncles)

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The specific feature of upper midbrain is presence of:
questions.explanation: The upper midbrain (superior colliculus level) has the crus cerebri (cerebral peduncle) on its ventral aspect, containing corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers. Substantia nigra and red nucleus are at this level but not specific to upper midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Upper midbrain specific feature: crus cerebri (cerebral peduncle)

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Sections In lower level of pons show.
questions.explanation: Sections at the lower level of pons show the MIDDLE cerebellar peduncle (the largest cerebellar peduncle, connecting pons to cerebellum). The superior cerebellar peduncle is more superior. The mesencephalic nucleus of V is in the midbrain. Medial and inferior vestibular nuclei are in the upper medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower pons: middle cerebellar peduncle. Midbrain: superior cerebellar peduncle. Medulla: inferior cerebellar peduncle.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The specific feature of upper mid brain is presence of:
questions.explanation: The SUPERIOR cerebellar peduncle DECUSSATION is specific to the upper midbrain - it carries cerebellar output to the thalamus. The crus cerebri and substantia nigra are present throughout the midbrain. Red nucleus is present in the upper midbrain but its decussation is not unique to upper level.
questions.keyConcept: Upper midbrain specific feature: decussation of superior cerebellar peduncles (dentatothalamic fibers).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Cells of Cajal are present in
questions.explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the MOLECULAR layer of the CEREBRAL cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface. In cerebellum, this layer contains Purkinje cells, not Cajal cells.
questions.keyConcept: Cajal cells: horizontal cells in molecular layer of cerebral cortex; horizontal axon orientation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Facilitation of stretch reflex is done by:
questions.explanation: Facilitation of stretch reflex is achieved by gamma motor neurons that contract intrafusal fibers, increasing spindle sensitivity and reflex excitability.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons facilitate stretch reflex by contracting intrafusal fibers and enhancing spindle discharge.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Brain stem includes all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The brain stem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. The cerebellum lies posterior to the brain stem and is not considered part of it, though it is connected by three peduncles.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellum not part of brain stem

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Hind brain (Rhombencephalon) includes all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes the medulla oblongata, pons, and cerebellum. The crus cerebri is part of the midbrain (not hindbrain), containing corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Crus cerebri is midbrain, not hindbrain

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The inferior cerebellar peduncle contains:
questions.explanation: The posterior (dorsal) spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the lower body to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. It does not decussate.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinocerebellar tract via inferior cerebellar peduncle

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: In memory:
options: Implicit memory is the conscious recall of information.
Explicit memory is stored in basal ganglia and cerebellum.
Explicit memory types include priming and procedural memory.
Episodic memory is stored in the hippocampus and neocortex.
Semantic memory is the recall of events and experiences.
questions.explanation: Episodic memory (remembering events) is stored in hippocampus and neocortex. Explicit memory IS conscious recall (not implicit). Implicit memory includes priming and procedural memory stored in basal ganglia/cerebellum. Semantic memory is general knowledge, not events.
questions.keyConcept: Explicit/declarative: conscious, hippocampus/neocortex. Implicit/non-declarative: unconscious, basal ganglia/cerebellum.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient has difficulty initiating movement, resting tremor, and cogwheel rigidity. Which structure is primarily affected?
questions.explanation: Parkinsonism features (difficulty initiating movement, resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity) result from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonism: substantia nigra degeneration.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following tracts carries the climbing fibers of cerebellum?
questions.explanation: Climbing fibers travel via the olivocerebellar tract through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to reach the cerebellum. The dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the trunk. The pontocerebellar tract carries mossy fibers from the pontine nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Olivocerebellar tract: inferior cerebellar peduncle → climbing fibers to cerebellum.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Parkinson's disease:
options: Is caused by a lesion in the substantia nigra.
Is caused by lesion in the posteroventral nucleus of the thalamus.
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is caused by lesion in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Option A is correct. The substantia nigra produces dopamine; its degeneration leads to dopamine deficiency in the striatum, causing Parkinsonian symptoms. Option B is wrong (thalamic lesions cause sensory symptoms, not Parkinsonism). Option C is wrong (Parkinsonism has resting tremors, not kinetic). Option D is wrong (clasp-knife rigidity is UMN, not Parkinsonian). Option E is wrong (pendular jerks are cerebellar).
questions.keyConcept: Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Compared to static tremors, intention tremors:
options: Are caused by loss of damping function of cerebellum.
Are characteristic to basal ganglia lesion.
questions.explanation: Intention tremors are caused by loss of damping function of cerebellum. Option C is correct. Intention (kinetic) tremor occurs when the cerebellum fails to dampen movements, worsening as target is approached. Options A, B, D describe static/rest tremors and basal ganglia: resting tremors occur in Parkinsonism, accompanied by hypertonia, and are characteristic of basal ganglia lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Intention tremor reflects cerebellar dysfunction in movement dampening and coordination feedback.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which is NOT a function of the cerebellum includes:
options: Stop the movement at the precise intended point.
questions.explanation: The cerebellum INHIBITS excess cortical activity, not inhibits cortical activity per se (which would be incorrect). Option E is poorly worded. Actually, the cerebellum projects to thalamus and cerebral cortex via the dentatothalamic pathway, modulating (facilitating or inhibiting) cortical motor areas. This helps fine-tune movements. The cerebellum doesn't directly inhibit cortical output but regulates it.
questions.keyConcept: The cerebellum modulates cortical motor output through the dentatothalamic pathway, regulating movement precision.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The declarative memory is described by which one of the following?
options: It can be remembered after thinking of related events
Recall of general facts is the episodic type
Memory of personal experiences is the semantic type
Its center is in hippocampus and cerebellum
It cannot be converted to non-declarative memory
questions.explanation: Declarative memory can be recalled by thinking of related events; it includes episodic (personal experiences) and semantic (general facts) components, primarily mediated by hippocampus.
questions.keyConcept: Declarative memory: recalled through related events, hippocampal.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Inferior olivary nucleus:
options: Present in the ventral aspect of closed medulla.
Its efferent fibers reach the ipsilateral cerebellar cortex through the superior cerebellar peduncle.
Its efferent fibers are the mousy fibers reaching the cerebellar cortex.
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus receives input from the red nucleus (rubro-olivary fibers). It is located in the OPEN medulla, not ventral aspect. Its efferent fibers decussate and reach the CONTRALATERAL cerebellar cortex through the INFERIOR cerebellar peduncle as climbing fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary: receives rubral input, in open medulla, projects via ICP to contralateral cerebellum as climbing fibers.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure is primarily responsible for the damping action that prevents tremors during voluntary movements?
questions.explanation: The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is responsible for the damping action that prevents overshoot and tremors during voluntary movements through its feedback loops.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar damping mechanism

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Dysdiadochokinesia is associated with lesions of the:
questions.explanation: Dysdiadochokinesia is associated with lesions of the cerebellum. Option C is correct. Inability to perform rapid alternating movements is a classic cerebellar sign. Options A, B, D are wrong (premotor, primary motor, basal ganglia lesions cause different symptoms).
questions.keyConcept: Dysdiadochokinesia (impaired rapid alternating movements) indicates cerebellar dysfunction.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning the nucleus dorsalis of Clark is TRUE?
options: It is found in the ventral horn.
It is present at all spinal levels.
It is homologous in function to the main sensory nucleus.
questions.explanation: The nucleus dorsalis of Clark projects to the cerebellum via the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, carrying proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and tendon organs. It is in the dorsal horn, present only at certain levels (C8-L3).
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus projects to cerebellum via dorsal spinocerebellar tract

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Parkinsonism:
options: A deficiency of dopamine in the substantia nigra.
A clasp-knife type of spastic rigidity.
Difficulty in initiating the voluntary movements.
questions.explanation: Clasp-knife spasticity is a pyramidal/UMN feature, NOT Parkinsonism. Option C is correct. Parkinsonian rigidity is lead-pipe or cogwheel type, not clasp-knife. Options A, B, D, E are all features of Parkinsonism: resting tremor, dopamine deficiency, difficulty initiating movements, and preserved reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonian rigidity is lead-pipe or cogwheel type, distinct from the clasp-knife spasticity of pyramidal lesions.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Mass reflex:
options: Has a pattern of rigidity of upper limbs.
Has a pattern of massive lower limb flexion with emptying of rectum and bladder.
Occurs immediately after spinal cord transcetion.
Is elicited by in patients with basal ganglia lesions.
questions.explanation: Mass reflex has pattern of massive lower limb flexion with emptying of rectum and bladder. Option B is correct. Mass reflex is a spinal reflex appearing after spinal shock resolution in complete transection; strong stimuli to skin trigger flexor withdrawal with autonomic discharge. Options A, C, D are incorrect (upper limb rigidity is wrong, immediate occurrence is wrong, basoganglia involvement is wrong).
questions.keyConcept: Mass reflex (flexor withdrawal with autonomic discharge) indicates complete spinal cord transection with recovered spinal reflexes.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Superior cerebellar peduncle contains which of the following tracts?
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle contains the ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract which carries proprioceptive feedback from the lower limbs to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle contains ventral spinocerebellar

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following surfaces (aspects) of thalamus is related to posterior limb of internal capsule?
questions.explanation: The lateral surface of the thalamus is related to the posterior limb of the internal capsule. The internal capsule carries corticospinal, corticopontine, thalamocortical, and corticothalamic fibers between the thalamus and the cerebral cortex. The superior thalamic surface relates to the body of lateral ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral surface of thalamus is related to posterior limb of internal capsule (contains thalamocortical and corticospinal fibers).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Concerning the basal ganglia function:
options: Caudate circuit helps execution of learned pattern of movement.
Putamen circuit is important for cognitive control of voluntary movements.
Caudate circuit terminates in motor area 4.
Damage to caudate circuit results in loss of timing and scaling of movements.
questions.explanation: Damage to caudate circuit results in loss of timing and scaling of movements. Option D is correct. The caudate circuit (caudate-putamen-GP-SNr-thalamus-caudate) is involved in movement scaling and timing. Option A is wrong (putamen executes learned patterns). Option B is wrong (caudate circuit is cognitive, putamen is motor). Option C is wrong (caudate circuit terminates in premotor, not motor area 4).
questions.keyConcept: Caudate nucleus circuits process movement scaling and timing through cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic loops.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient shows ipsilateral tongue atrophy, contralateral loss of vibration, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature of the body. The lesion is in the:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (CN XII, medial lemniscus, pyramid).
questions.keyConcept: Tongue deviation toward lesion with ipsilateral atrophy: hypoglossal nerve lesion.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Adiadochokinesia:
options: Is failure of the patient to perform rapid coordinate movements.
Is due to lesion in caudate nucleus.
Is due to lesion in subthalamus.
Is due to lesion in vestibulocerebellum.
questions.explanation: Adiadochokinesia is failure to perform rapid alternating movements. Option A is correct. This is a classic cerebellar sign. It is due to lesion in the cerebellum (especially neocerebellum). Options B, C, D are wrong (caudate, subthalamus, vestibulocerebellum lesions cause different symptoms). Cerebellar lesions cause hypotonia, not hypertonia (option E is wrong).
questions.keyConcept: Inability to perform rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia) indicates cerebellar dysfunction.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following maneuvers will weakens the stretch reflex in skeletal muscle?
options: Sectioning the dorsal root of a spinal nerve
Sectioning the medial lemniscus on the contralateral side of the skeletal muscle in question
Creating a lesion in the contralateral globus pallidus
questions.explanation: Sectioning the dorsal root eliminates the afferent limb of the stretch reflex (Ia fibers from muscle spindles), causing immediate weakening or loss of the reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root sectioning: weakens stretch reflex by cutting afferent limb.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Fibers of vagus nerve exit ….
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) exits the brainstem between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle, at the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla. This is the same level where glossopharyngeal and accessary nerves also emerge.
questions.keyConcept: Vagus nerve: exits between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle at posterolateral sulcus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards medulla oblongata, choose the INCORRECT statement:
options: Olive lies just lateral to anterior median fissure.
Inferior cerebellar peduncle lies lateral to olive.
XII cranial nerve exits from medulla lateral to pyramid.
X cranial nerve lies medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle.
XI cranial nerve is attached to posterolateral sulcus.
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) lies MEDIAL to the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Rootlets emerge between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle. The statement in option D incorrectly places it lateral to ICP.
questions.keyConcept: Vagus nerve medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which function is performed by the cerebellum?
options: Correct movement on the same side of the body
Initiation of voluntary movement on the same side
Coordination of opposite side limb movements
questions.explanation: The cerebellum corrects movements on the same side of the body through its deep cerebellar nuclei and their projections to the thalamus and motor cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Ipsilateral cerebellar function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Contents of interpeduncular fossa belong to:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is located in the midbrain, between the cerebral peduncles. Its contents (oculomotor nerve, posterior perforated substance, etc.) are all midbrain structures.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa belongs to midbrain

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Brain stem includes the following Except
questions.explanation: The brain stem includes midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata; the cerebellum and cerebral aqueduct are not part of the brain stem proper (cerebral aqueduct connects third and fourth ventricles).
questions.keyConcept: Brain stem structural components

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient complains of unsteadiness during that is profound during darkness. Examination shows a marked diminution of position sense, vibration sense, and stereognosis of all extremities. He is unable to stand without wavering for more than a few seconds when his eyes are closed. There are no other abnormal findings. The lesion most likely involves the:
options: Lateral columns of the spinal cord, bilaterally
Dorsal columns of the spinal cord, bilaterally
questions.explanation: Bilateral dorsal column lesion causes loss of proprioception, vibration sense, and stereognosis in all extremities, with a positive Romberg sign (falls when eyes closed because proprioception is lost). The patient uses visual input to compensate, hence the profound unsteadiness in darkness. Spinocerebellar tract lesions cause ataxia but not sensory loss; lateral column lesions affect corticospinal tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Bilateral dorsal column lesion = loss of proprioception/vibration/stereognosis, positive Romberg; profound unsteadiness in darkness because vision cannot compensate.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Parkinson's disease is characterized by:
options: Paralysis of one side of the body.
Increase of dopamine in the substantia nigra.
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is characterized by lead-pipe rigidity. Option D is correct. The resting tremor worsens with action (not at rest as stated in option A). Paralysis is not a feature (option B is wrong). Dopamine is decreased, not increased (option C is wrong). Clonus is not a Parkinsonian feature (option E is wrong). Lead-pipe rigidity with cogwheel phenomenon is pathognomonic.
questions.keyConcept: Lead-pipe rigidity is the characteristic motor sign of Parkinson's disease, with constant resistance throughout passive movement.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: About substantia nigra, all true except:
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra is present DORSAL to the cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri), not ventral. It consists of pars compacta (dopaminergic neurons) and pars reticularis. It is connected to the basal ganglia circuit. Its dopamine content gives it its dark color.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia nigra: dorsal to crus cerebri, contains dopamine, connected to basal ganglia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following structures forms the roof of the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The roof of the fourth ventricle consists of the superior cerebellar peduncles laterally and the tela choroidea with choroid plexus inferiorly. The floor is formed by the pons and upper medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof comprises cerebellar peduncles and tela choroidea with choroid plexus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which one of the following decussations is associated with red nucleus?
options: Decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.explanation: The decussation associated with the red nucleus is the ventral tegmental decussation (also called decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle). The red nucleus gives rise to the rubrospinal tract which decussates in the ventral tegmentum of the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral tegmental decussation is associated with red nucleus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The following is / are correctly matched with areas of dopamine blockade:
questions.explanation: Dopamine blockade in different brain regions produces different effects: 1) Extrapyramidal effects (EPS) occur from D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway (basal ganglia) - TRUE; 2) Antipsychotic effect occurs from blockade in mesolimbic pathway - TRUE; 3) Antiemetic effect occurs from blockade in chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) - TRUE. Since all statements are correct, D (all of the above) is the correct answer. This is a classic concept: the same drug (antipsychotic) produces different effects depending on which dopamine pathway is blocked.
questions.keyConcept: Antipsychotic effects depend on dopamine blockade location: mesolimbic (antipsychotic), nigrostriatal (EPS), CTZ (antiemetic).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards pathway of fine touch, choose the CORRECT statement:
options: Its 1st neuron terminates in posterior horn of spinal cord.
Its 2nd neuron form external arcuate fibers.
Its fibers ascend in brain stem within spinal lemniscus.
VPMN of thalamus forms its 3rd neuron.
Its fibers pass through posterior limb of internal capsule.
questions.explanation: Fine touch pathway: 1st neuron (dorsal root ganglion) ascends in dorsal columns to gracile/cuneate nuclei; 2nd neuron decussates as internal arcuate fibers and ascends in medial lemniscus (not spinal lemniscus) to VPL (not VPM) of thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Fine touch uses medial lemniscus, not spinal lemniscus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following tracts is present in all segments of spinal cord?
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract is present in all spinal cord segments, carrying proprioceptive information from lower limbs to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract present in all spinal cord segments

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 25-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of difficulty paying attention. He reports that he has been having trouble staying focused on tasks and remembering things for the past few months. He also has difficulty controlling his impulses and making decisions. Which of the following anatomical areas of the brain is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation: The frontal lobe is responsible for executive functions including attention, working memory, impulse control, decision-making, and social behavior. Difficulty staying focused, remembering things, and controlling impulses indicates frontal lobe dysfunction. The prefrontal cortex is particularly important for these higher cognitive functions. The parietal lobe processes sensation; the cerebellum coordinates movement.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe = executive functions (attention, memory, impulse control, decision-making); damage causes frontal lobe syndrome.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The hypoglossal nerve:
options: Emerges from medulla between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Leaves the skull through jugular foramen.
Lies within the upper part of carotid sheath.
Is joined by a branch from C2.
It sensory to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits the skull through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen. It carries C1 spinal nerve fibers that branch off to supply the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles. CN XII does NOT lie within the carotid sheath (it crosses superficially over it), is NOT joined by C2, is purely motor (NOT sensory), and emerges between the pyramid and the olive (not between the olive and ICP).
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve carries C1 fibers and supplies thyrohyoid and geniohyoid; joined by branch from C1 not C2.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which tract carries unconscious proprioception from the lower limb to the cerebellum without crossing?
questions.explanation: The posterior spinocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioceptive information from the lower limb directly to the cerebellum on the same side without crossing, originating from Clarke's nucleus at T1-L2.
questions.keyConcept: Unconscious proprioception from lower limb: posterior spinocerebellar tract, uncrossed.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Thalamic nucleus that relays basal ganglia output:
questions.explanation: The ventral anterior (VA) nucleus is the thalamic relay for basal ganglia output. It receives input from the internal segment of the globus pallidus (medial GPi) and projects to the premotor and supplementary motor cortices. This pathway is important for motor planning and sequencing of movements.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral anterior nucleus relays basal ganglia output (from GPi) to premotor cortex.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which tract passes through the superior cerebellar peduncle?
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle contains primarily efferent fibers from the dentate nucleus to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus (dentatorubrothalamic pathway), carrying cerebellar output.
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle is the major output pathway from cerebellum to forebrain.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The most lateral nucleus in the interior of the cerebellum is:
questions.explanation: The dentate nucleus is the largest and most lateral cerebellar nucleus. It receives input from the cerebellar cortex (particularly the lateral parts) and projects via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the thalamus and red nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Dentate nucleus is most lateral, projects via SCP

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The falx cerebri
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri separates the cerebral hemispheres and contains the superior sagittal sinus in its superior border; the diaphragma sellae separates the pituitary from the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri anatomy

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The idea of the voluntary movement is generated in which one of the following:
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex generates the idea and plan for voluntary movement, while the primary motor cortex executes the movement and supplementary motor area prepares for it.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal cortex generates the idea of voluntary movement.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure is found at the level of the open medulla?
questions.explanation: The open medulla at the level of the decussation of the medial lemniscus contains structures like the inferior olivary nucleus, the vagus nucleus, and the nucleus tractus solitarius.
questions.keyConcept: Open medulla contains cranial nerve nuclei (IX, X) and inferior olivary nucleus at this level.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The crossed corticospinal tract occupies the:
options: Lateral white column of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract occupies the lateral white column of the spinal cord. It is the continuation of the pyramidal decussation and controls voluntary movement of the contralateral limbs.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral corticospinal tract in lateral white column

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Cells of Cajal are present in:
questions.explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the molecular layer (layer I) of the cerebral cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface.
questions.keyConcept: Cells of Cajal in molecular layer of cerebral cortex (layer I)

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Cerebellar cortex:
options: Contain martonitti cells in the molecular layer.
Is of uniform structure all over cerebellum
questions.explanation: The cerebellar cortex is NOT uniform - different regions have different afferent inputs (vestibular, spinocerebellar, corticocerebellar). It has 3 layers (molecular, Purkinje, granular), not 6. It does show sulci (folia).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar cortex: 3 layers (molecular, Purkinje, granular), folia/sulci, non-uniform structure.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Static tremor is caused by which mechanism in the basal ganglia?
options: Loss of dopamine in substantia nigra
Oscillation between GPi and subthalamic nucleus
questions.explanation: Static (resting) tremor in Parkinson's disease results from oscillatory activity between the globus pallidus interna and subthalamic nucleus due to loss of dopamine.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonian tremor mechanism

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure is part of the neostriatum?
questions.explanation: The neostriatum consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen (also called the striatum). It receives cortical input and dopaminergic input from the substantia nigra pars compacta.
questions.keyConcept: Neostriatum comprises caudate and putamen, the major input structures of the basal ganglia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Anterior cerebral artery supplies all the following EXCEPT:
options: Most of medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere.
Medial aspect of orbital part of inferior surface of the hemisphere.
All anterior limb of internal capsule.
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial cerebral surface, orbital inferior surface, and genu of internal capsule, but the anterior limb is supplied by the middle cerebral artery via perforating branches.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery supplies medial surface and genu, not anterior limb of internal capsule.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 45-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of difficulty walking. He reports that he has been having trouble balancing and coordinating his movements for the past few months. He also has difficulty judging distances and reaching for objects. Which of the following anatomical areas of the brain is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation: Difficulty balancing, coordinating movements, and judging distances (dysmetria) are classic signs of cerebellar dysfunction. The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movements, maintains balance, and regulates muscle tone. Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria, and dysarthria. The frontal lobe controls motor planning; the parietal lobe processes sensation.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar lesion = ataxia (difficulty balancing/coordinating), dysmetria (difficulty judging distances), intention tremor.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The descending tracts run in the following part of the midbrain:
questions.explanation: The descending tracts (corticospinal, corticobulbar) run in the crus cerebri of the midbrain. The tegmentum contains ascending tracts and nuclei. The substantia nigra separates the crus from the tegmentum.
questions.keyConcept: Descending tracts in crus cerebri

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Cuneate tract:
options: Its main 2nd neuron is the accessory cuneate nucleus.
Its 3rd neuron passes in the anterior limb of the internal capsule.
Its 3rd neuron terminates in the precentral gyrus.
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract begins at the C8 spinal segment and carries conscious proprioception and fine touch from the upper limb. It does not start at mid-thoracic region—that level marks the beginning of the gracile tract.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract starts at C8, carries upper limb proprioception

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient suffering from damage of basal ganglia may NOT show:
questions.explanation: Basal ganglia lesions do NOT cause hyperreflexia and clonus - these are UMN signs. Option B is correct. The basal ganglia lesions cause hypokinetic movements (hypokinesia), shuffling gait, and tremor, but not hyperreflexia. Option A is wrong (static tremors occur in basal ganglia lesions). Option C is wrong (shuffling gait is a feature). Option D is wrong (degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra is the cause of Parkinson's). Option E is wrong (hypokinesia does occur).
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia lesions cause hypokinetic features (hypokinesia, shuffling gait) with normal or decreased reflexes, not hyperreflexia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The reward center is in which one of the following?
questions.explanation: The reward (pleasure) center is located in the lateral hypothalamus; stimulation produces feelings of satisfaction and reinforces behaviors necessary for survival.
questions.keyConcept: Reward center: lateral hypothalamus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Retrolentiform part of internal capsule DOESN'T transmit:
questions.explanation: The retrolentiform part of internal capsule contains visual radiation, occipito-pontine, and parieto-pontine fibers, but the auditory radiation passes through the sublentiform part.
questions.keyConcept: Retrolentiform: visual/occipito-parieto-pontine fibers; auditory goes sublentiform.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient develops contralateral loss of pain and temperature of the body with ipsilateral facial signs. The occluded vessel is the:
options: Superior cerebellar artery supplying the upper cerebellum
questions.explanation: PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Contralateral pain and temperature loss below lesion: lateral spinothalamic tract lesion.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) coordinates movements between which structures?
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) connects the vestibular nuclei to the abducens and oculomotor nuclei, coordinating eye movements with head movements in the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
questions.keyConcept: MLF coordinates eyes and head via vestibulo-ocular reflex.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Arterial supply of upper 1/2 of internal capsule is derived from:
questions.explanation: Upper half of internal capsule is supplied by central branches of anterior cerebral artery; lower half receives branches from anterior choroidal and posterior communicating arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule upper half supply

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The anterior thalamic nucleus is connected to the:
questions.explanation: The anterior thalamic nucleus receives major input from the mammillary bodies via the mammillothalamic tract. The mammillary bodies receive input from the hippocampus via the fornix, completing the Papez circuit of the limbic system. It also projects back to the hippocampus indirectly.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior thalamic nucleus is connected to hypothalamus via mammillothalamic tract and Papez circuit.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding the cerebellum, which is NOT true:
options: Cerebellum helps in planning and timing of voluntary movements.
The cerebellum is stimulated by the motor cortex.
The receptor activity of the spindles and Golgi tendons organs reaches the cerebellum through the spinocerebellar tract.
The cerebellum has direct stimulatory effect on alpha motor neurons.
The cerebellum predicts and plans for the successive movements
questions.explanation: The cerebellum has INDIRECT stimulatory effect on alpha motor neurons via the red nucleus and thalamus, not direct. Option D is incorrect. Options A, B, C, E are all true: cerebellum helps plan and time movements, receives input from motor cortex, receives spindle/GTO input via spinocerebellar tracts, and predicts successive movements.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar influence on motor neurons is indirect, acting through the red nucleus and thalamus to modulate cortical output.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Rootlets of hypoglossal nerve lie:
options: Between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Between lower border of pons & pyramid.
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve rootlets emerge from the anterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the pyramid and olive. This is the anterior surface of the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: CN XII between pyramid and olive

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Corticonuclear fibers pass through ……… of internal capsule to reach the brain stem.
questions.explanation: Corticonuclear fibers (corticobulbar tract) pass through the genu (bend) of the internal capsule to reach brainstem cranial nerve nuclei for voluntary control of face and neck muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Corticonuclear fibers pass through genu of internal capsule.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Hind brain (Rhombencephalon) includes the following Except
questions.explanation: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes medulla oblongata, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle; the crus cerebri is part of the midbrain (mesencephalon), not hindbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Hindbrain components

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which one of the following is NOT true regarding the cerebellum:
options: Each cerebellar hemisphere controls movements of the ipsilateral muscles.
Cerebellar ataxia is a sensory ataxia.
Cerebellar lesions cause pendular knee jerks.
The intention tremor associated with cerebellar disease is worsened by movement.
The neocerebellar syndrome gait is zig-zag like.
questions.explanation: Cerebellar ataxia is sensory ataxia - it worsens with eye closure (positive Romberg). Option B is INCORRECT as stated. Actually, cerebellar ataxia is NOT sensory (sensory ataxia is dorsal column dysfunction). The correct answer is B because cerebellar ataxia is motor ataxia, characterized by clumsiness that is visible with eyes open, unlike sensory ataxia which hides behind visual compensation. Wait - re-reading: cerebellar ataxia is a motor (not sensory) ataxia that DOES NOT require visual compensation to demonstrate.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar ataxia is a motor coordination deficit visible even with eyes open, unlike sensory ataxia which requires eye closure to manifest.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which fibers enter the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle?
questions.explanation: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries afferent fibers including the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's column), cuneocerebellar fibers, and vestibulocerebellar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior cerebellar peduncle is primarily afferent, carrying proprioceptive and vestibular information to cerebellum.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding servocomparator function of the cerebellum:
options: Cerebellum sends direct corrective messages to muscles.
Cerebellum compares the intended plan of movement with the actual movement.
Cerebellum receives feedback information from muscles through conscious proprioceptive receptors.
Cerebellum receives a copy of plan of movement from basal ganglia.
questions.explanation: Cerebellum compares intended plan with actual movement (servocomparator function). Option B is correct. The cerebellum receives copies of motor commands (efference copy) and actual movement feedback, comparing them to correct ongoing movements. Options A, C, D are wrong: cerebellum sends indirect (via thalamus) not direct messages; receives unconscious (not conscious) proprioception; receives plan from cortex not basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: The cerebellum acts as a servocomparator, matching intended movement with actual execution through continuous feedback.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Afferent fibers in the superior cerebellar peduncle include:
questions.explanation: The anterior (ventral) spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the lower body to the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle. It decussates twice (once at the level of entry and once before entering the cerebellum).
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinocerebellar enters via superior cerebellar peduncle

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Spasticity is characterized by:
options: Due to increase alpha and gamma cells activities.
questions.explanation: Spasticity is of clasp-knife nature. Option E is correct. Clasp-knife spasticity is velocity-dependent increased tone with sudden release, characteristic of UMN lesions. Options A, B, C, D are incorrect: spasticity affects antigravity muscles primarily; is due to UMN (not basal ganglia) lesions; is associated with static/resting tremors (Parkinsonian); and clonus is not defining characteristic.
questions.keyConcept: Clasp-knife spasticity is the hallmark of corticospinal (upper motor neuron) lesions, with sudden release after initial resistance.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Rootlets of glossopharyngeal nerve lie:
options: Between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Between lower border of pons and medulla.
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve rootlets emerge from the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Dorsal spinocerebellar enters cerebellum through ............. while ventral spinocerebellar through.............
options: Superior cerebellar peduncle, inferior cerebellar peduncle
inferior cerebellar peduncle, superior cerebellar peduncle
questions.explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract enters via the inferior cerebellar peduncle while the ventral spinocerebellar tract enters via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar peduncle entries

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is the best choice for patients with dementia due to substantia nigra lesion (Parkinson’s disease)?
questions.explanation: Rivastigmine is a centrally acting cholinesterase inhibitor FDA‑approved for dementia associated with Parkinson's disease, targeting the cholinergic deficit caused by basal forebrain degeneration.
questions.keyConcept: Rivastigmine is the cholinesterase inhibitor of choice for Parkinson's disease dementia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Concerning cerebellum:
options: Each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates the contralateral muscles.
Spinocerebellar tracts give rise to conscious recognition of joint position sense.
Paleocerbellar is facilitatory to muscle tone.
Cerebellar ataxia is associated with spasticity.
questions.explanation: Neocerebellum helps planning of movements. Option D is correct. The neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) receives input from motor and premotor cortex and helps in movement planning and timing. Option A is wrong (each hemisphere controls ipsilateral muscles). Option B is wrong (spinocerebellar tracts provide unconscious proprioception). Option C is wrong (paleocerebellum调节肌张力). Option E is wrong (cerebellar ataxia has hypotonia, not spasticity).
questions.keyConcept: The neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is crucial for movement planning and coordination with the motor cortex.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Axon in proprioception ascend in:
questions.explanation: Proprioception fibers from the thalamus ascend via the posterior limb of the internal capsule (along with other sensory fibers) to the primary somatosensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule somatosensory fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The floor of the body of the lateral ventricle is formed by all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The floor of the lateral ventricle body is formed by the thalamus, body of caudate nucleus, and body of fornix; the tail of caudate lies in the roof of the inferior horn, not the floor.
questions.keyConcept: Tail of caudate nucleus: in roof of inferior horn, not floor of body.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: At which anatomical level does the oculomotor nerve emerge?
options: At the level of the superior midbrain colliculus
At the level of the inferior olivary nucleus
At the level of the pons
At the level of the medullary pyramids
At the level of the cerebellar peduncles
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges from the midbrain on the anterior surface between the cerebral peduncles, just posterior to the posterior clinoid process.
questions.keyConcept: CN III emerges from the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles on the anterior surface.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All characters of dorsal spinocerebellar tract except:
options: ascending in white matter then closed medulla then end in cerebellum
carry impulse from lower limb only on same side
carry impulse from lower limb, trunk in opposite side
questions.explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries impulses from the lower limb and trunk on the ipsilateral side (after crossing once in the spinal cord via Clarke's nucleus).
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Glutamate is secreted by:
questions.explanation: Corticostriatal fibers (cortex to corpus striatum) use glutamate as their neurotransmitter, providing the major excitatory input to the striatum.
questions.keyConcept: Corticostriatal projection

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Falx cerebri:
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process.
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is a fold of dura mater between the cerebral hemispheres, attached to the crista galli anteriorly and the tentorium cerebelli posteriorly. It contains the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri is dura between hemispheres

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which fibers are afferent to cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle?
questions.explanation: Afferents through the inferior cerebellar peduncle include: dorsal spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's column), cuneocerebellar fibers from accessory cuneate nucleus, and vestibulocerebellar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior cerebellar peduncle carries proprioceptive and vestibular afferents to cerebellum.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the pyramidal tract, choose the INCORRECT statement:
options: It arises mainly from motor & premotor areas.
It passes in posterior limb of internal capsule.
It descends as a compact bundle in basis pontis.
Its crossed fibers form lateral corticospinal tract.
In spinal cord, its cervical fibers are medial.
questions.explanation: The pyramidal tract descends as a compact bundle in the medullary pyramids, not scattered. The scattering occurs only in the basis pontis due to crossing pontocerebellar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Pyramidal tract compact in medulla, scattered in pons

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Concerning the interpeduncular fossa, one of the following is a boundary of the fossa:
questions.explanation: The optic tract forms the lateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa; the cerebral peduncles form the posterior boundary.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa boundaries

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The falx cerebri:
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process.
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri: a dura mater fold between cerebral hemispheres, attached to crista galli anteriorly and tentorium posteriorly, contains superior sagittal sinus.选项B正确. The answer is B. It prevents hemisphere displacement.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri: dura fold between hemispheres, contains superior sagittal sinus - prevents midline shift.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient complains of tremors in the right hand while doing fine movements. When asked to walk along a straight line on the floor, the patient sways over to the right side. When asked to touch his nose with his right index finger, the right hand displays tremor, and the finger tends to overshoot the target. At surgery, he is found to have tumour. Locate the possible site of tumour.
questions.explanation: Intention tremor, overshoot (dysmetria), and swaying to the right during gait indicate a right cerebellar lesion; the tumor is in the right cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar lesion signs

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Select the correct answer about lateral corticospinal tract:
options: Most of its fibers arise from precentral gyrus.
Passes in anterior limb of internal capsule.
Its injury produces a lower motor neuron lesion.
questions.explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract arises mainly from the precentral gyrus (primary motor area, Brodmann area 4). Its fibers decussate in the pyramidal decussation of the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral corticospinal arises from precentral gyrus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: What is the aim of drug therapy in Parkinson’s disease?
options: To restore balance between dopamine and acetylcholine activity in the basal ganglia
To increase dopamine activity in the basal ganglia
To decrease acetylcholine activity in the basal ganglia
questions.explanation: The aim of drug therapy in Parkinson's disease is to restore dopamine deficiency and reduce excess cholinergic activity. This involves: dopamine replacement (L-dopa, dopamine agonists), COMT inhibitors (entacapone), MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline), and anticholinergics for tremor.选项A正确. The answer is A. Treatment aims to improve motor symptoms and quality of life.
questions.keyConcept: PD drug therapy aims to restore dopaminergic activity and reduce cholinergic excess - improving motor function.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the pyramidal tract, choose the CORRECT statement:
options: It arises from motor area 4 only.
It passes through anterior limb of internal capsule.
It descends within the medial 3/5 of basis pedunculi.
It descends as scattered bundles in basis pontis.
Its crossed fibers in medulla form anterior corticospinal tract.
questions.explanation: The corticospinal fibers descend as scattered bundles in the basis pontis because they are interrupted by transverse pontine fibers. This is a normal anatomical feature of the pontine base.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal scattered in pons by pontine fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Vertebrobasilar system supplies the following Except:
questions.explanation: Vertebrobasilar system supplies cerebellum, inner ear (labyrinthine artery), occipital cortex (PCA), and pons; the temporal pole is supplied by MCA, not vertebrobasilar.
questions.keyConcept: Vertebrobasilar territories

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: L1 spinal cord segment lies at level of which one of following vertebra:
questions.explanation: In adults, the spinal cord ends at L1–L2, and the vertebral level is approximately 2–3 segments higher than the spinal cord segment at lower levels. The L1 cord segment lies at the T10 vertebral level.
questions.keyConcept: L1 spinal cord segment ≈ T10 vertebral level

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Compression of which segment of the spinal cord would occur by a tumor at 4th thoracic vertebra?
questions.explanation: There is a discrepancy between vertebral and spinal cord levels in the thoracic region. The spinal cord segments are approximately 2 levels higher than their corresponding vertebrae in the lower thoracic region. A tumor at T4 would compress the T6 spinal cord segment.
questions.keyConcept: Lower thoracic spinal cord segments are ~2 vertebral levels higher than the vertebrae

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: At birth the spinal cord ends at the level of:
options: Lower border of the 1st lumbar vertebra.
Upper border of the 2nd lumbar vertebra.
Upper border of the 3rd lumbar vertebra.
questions.explanation: At birth, the spinal cord extends to the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). Due to differential growth of the vertebral column, the cord ascends to L1–L2 in adults.
questions.keyConcept: Neonatal spinal cord ends at L3; adult at L1–L2

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A disc prolapsed between T5 and T6 vertebrae would exert pressure upon:
questions.explanation: In the thoracic region, the intervertebral disc is located above the corresponding numbered nerve root because the nerve exits below the pedicle of the same-numbered vertebra. Therefore, a disc prolapse between T5 and T6 would compress the T6 nerve root as it exits.
questions.keyConcept: Thoracic disc herniation at T5–T6 compresses the T6 nerve root

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The nerve(s) that emerge from the vertebral canal above the corresponding vertebrae are:
questions.explanation: The first seven cervical nerves (C1–C7) emerge above their corresponding vertebrae. C8 emerges between C7 and T1. All other spinal nerves emerge below their corresponding vertebrae.
questions.keyConcept: C1–C7 nerves emerge above their corresponding vertebrae

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The upper 9 thoracic vertebrae contain:
options: Upper 6 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
Upper 8 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
Upper 10 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
Lower 10 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
All thoracic segments of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Due to the cephalad ascent of the spinal cord relative to the vertebral column during development, the upper 9 thoracic vertebrae contain the upper 10 thoracic spinal cord segments. There is approximately a 1–2 segment discrepancy.
questions.keyConcept: Upper 9 thoracic vertebrae house the upper 10 thoracic cord segments

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: How many segments of the spinal cord lie in the vertebral column above the level of lower border of 4th thoracic vertebra (T4)?
questions.explanation: The spinal cord segments above the level of the lower border of the fourth thoracic vertebra include 8 cervical + 4 thoracic = 12 segments.
questions.keyConcept: 12 spinal cord segments lie above T4 vertebral level

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: How many segments of the spinal cord lie in the vertebral column above the level of lower border of 9th thoracic vertebra (T9)?
questions.explanation: Above the lower border of the ninth thoracic vertebra, the spinal cord contains 8 cervical + 9 thoracic = 17 segments. Due to differential growth, the cord segments are higher than their corresponding vertebrae.
questions.keyConcept: 17 spinal cord segments lie above the T9 vertebral level

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the dorsal root fibers of spinal nerves, choose the CORRECT statement:
options: Cells of dorsal root ganglion are multipolar.
Central processes (dendrites) of dorsal root fibers are connected to receptors.
Dorsal root fibers give ascending fibers which form long tracts.
Dorsal root fibers give long descending fibers.
After entering spinal cord, dorsal root fibers give long fibers which form intersegmental tracts.
questions.explanation: The dorsal root ganglion cells are pseudounipolar (not multipolar). The central processes (axons) of dorsal root ganglion cells enter the spinal cord and may ascend or descend to form long tracts. The peripheral processes (dendrites) connect to receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root ganglion cells are pseudounipolar; central processes form ascending tracts

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the nuclei of the posterior horn of the spinal cord, choose the INCORRECT matching:
options: Posteromarginal nucleus - tip of posterior horn.
Nucleus proprius - lies anterior to substantia gelatinosa.
Posterior commissural nuclei - form intersegmental tracts.
Intermediomedial nucleus - serves in transmission of visceral afferent impulses.
Reticular nucleus - lies medial to nucleus proprius.
questions.explanation: The intermediomedial nucleus is associated with the lateral horn and visceral afferent fibers, not the posterior horn. The posteromarginal nucleus is at the tip of the posterior horn. Nucleus proprius lies anterior to substantia gelatinosa.
questions.keyConcept: Intermediomedial nucleus belongs to the lateral horn, not the posterior horn

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards lamina of spinal cord, choose the INCORRECT matching:
options: Lamina II - corresponds to substantia gelatinosa.
Lamina III - corresponds to main sensory nucleus.
Lamina IV - corresponds to reticular nucleus.
Lamina VIII - receives termination of extrapyramidal tracts.
questions.explanation: Lamina IV corresponds to the nucleus proprius (main sensory nucleus), not the reticular nucleus. The reticular nucleus corresponds to lamina V. Lamina II = substantia gelatinosa, lamina III = nucleus proprius, lamina VII includes Clarke's nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Lamina IV = nucleus proprius; lamina V = reticular nucleus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The fibers present in the medial 1/5 of the crus cerebri are:
questions.explanation: The frontal pontine fibers (from prefrontal cortex) occupy the medial one-fifth of the crus cerebri. Corticospinal fibers are in the middle three-fifths, and parieto/temporopontine fibers are in the lateral one-fifth.
questions.keyConcept: Frontopontine fibers in medial 1/5 of crus cerebri

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the prevertebral fascia, choose the INCORRECT statement:
options: It is related anteriorly to pharynx.
It is attached superiorly to base of skull.
It lies infront of Scalenus medius.
questions.explanation: The prevertebral fascia covers the prevertebral muscles (longus colli, longus capitis) and scalene muscles (anterior, medius, posterior). It is attached superiorly to the base of the skull, extends laterally to form the axillary sheath, and lies in front of (anterior to) the prevertebral muscles. The prevertebral fascia does NOT lie in front of the trachea; that is the preTRACHEAL fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Prevertebral fascia covers prevertebral muscles, NOT trachea (that's pretracheal fascia).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All are true regarding atlanto-occipital joint Except:
options: Its anterior membrane is a continuation of ant. longitudinal ligament.
Its posterior membrane is similar to the ligamentum flavum.
questions.explanation: The atlanto-occipital joint does NOT allow rotation of the head—rotation occurs at the atlanto-axial joints. It is a condylar (ellipsoidal) synovial joint allowing flexion/extension and lateral bending. The anterior atlanto-occipital membrane is a continuation of the anterior longitudinal ligament; the posterior membrane is similar to the ligamentum flavum.
questions.keyConcept: Atlanto-occipital joint is synovial condylar; allows flexion/extension but NOT rotation. Anterior membrane = continuation of ALL; posterior membrane = like ligamentum flavum.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 5-day-old child has been treated in the intensive care unit since birth. A sample of cerebral spinal fluid is required. Where would be the safest place to perform a lumbar puncture?
questions.explanation: In a 5-day-old infant, the spinal cord ends at L3 (newborn level). Lumbar puncture below L3 (between L4 and L5) is safe because the spinal cord has already ended, avoiding risk of cord injury. In adults, the safe lumbar puncture level is L3-L4 or L4-L5. Needles below L3 in newborns avoid the terminated cord.
questions.keyConcept: In newborns, spinal cord ends at L3; safest lumbar puncture = below L3 (e.g., L4-L5) to avoid cord injury.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Complete section of spinal cord above C5 results in
questions.explanation: Complete transection of the spinal cord above C5 results in quadriplegia (paralysis of all four limbs) due to interruption of all descending motor pathways at the cervical level, along with respiratory compromise.
questions.keyConcept: C5 cord transection quadriplegia

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Arterial supply of anterior ends of caudate & lentiform nuclei is derived from:
questions.explanation: Anterior cerebral artery central branches supply anterior portions of caudate nucleus and lentiform nucleus, forming lenticulostriate arteries that also supply internal capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral central branches

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Nerve group cell with same origin, function inside CNS:
questions.explanation: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers with the same origin, course, and termination within the CNS, such as the corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: CNS tract definition

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Commissural Nuclei is between:
questions.explanation: Commissural nuclei connect sensory and motor nuclei on opposite sides of the spinal cord, facilitating crossed reflexes and coordinated movement.
questions.keyConcept: Commissural nuclei

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Medial longitudinal bundle continue in spinal cord through:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus continues in the spinal cord via the vestibulospinal and sulcomarginal tracts, coordinating head-eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: MLF continuation

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: External arcuate fibres carry impulses to:
questions.explanation: External arcuate fibers carry proprioceptive and vestibular information to the cerebellum via the peduncles, forming the mossy fiber input.
questions.keyConcept: External arcuate fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: An injury to the posterior column of the lumbar spinal cord may be manifested as loss of:
options: fine touch at the upper limbs.
tactile discrimination at the lower limbs
crude touch at the upper limbs
pain & temperature at the lower limbs
questions.explanation: Posterior column lesion at lumbar level causes loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception (tactile discrimination) in the ipsilateral lower limbs.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior column lesion

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which lamina of the spinal cord corresponds to the substantia gelatinosa?
questions.explanation: Substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) corresponds to Rexed lamina II of the posterior horn, specializing in pain and temperature modulation.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia gelatinosa lamina

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: In a complete spinal cord transection at the level of T6, which of the following would be expected?
options: Loss of pain sensation from the upper limbs
questions.explanation: A complete transection at T6 would cause paraplegia (paralysis of both lower limbs) since this level is below the cervical region and does not affect upper limb innervation or respiratory muscles.
questions.keyConcept: T6 transection: paraplegia of both lower limbs.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The axillary sheath is an extension from ……… fascia.
questions.explanation: The axillary sheath is an extension of the prevertebral fascia (from the anterior vertebral muscles) that surrounds the axillary vessels and brachial plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Axillary sheath: extension of prevertebral fascia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: UMNL of cranial nerves can result from cerebrovascular accident affecting ……… artery.
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies medial frontal and parietal regions including motor cortex areas controlling lower limbs; CVA here causes contralateral leg weakness and UMN signs.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery: UMN lesion of cranial nerves (if affecting cortical areas).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The neocerebellum is anatomically located in the following part of the cerebellum:
questions.explanation: The neocerebellum (lateral parts of posterior lobe) is anatomically located in the posterior lobe of the cerebellum. It is concerned with planning and executing voluntary movements, particularly those requiring skilled precision.
questions.keyConcept: Neocerebellum in posterior lobe

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which cerebellar structures are separated by fissura prima?
questions.explanation: The fissura prima separates the anterior and posterior lobes of the cerebellum. It divides the culmen (anterior lobe) from the declive, folium, and tuber (posterior lobe).
questions.keyConcept: Fissura prima divides the anterior and posterior cerebellar lobes, separating motor from non-motor regions.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which function is primarily controlled by the flocculonodular lobe of the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) primarily regulates balance and eye movements through connections with the vestibular nuclei. Lesions cause ataxia and nystagmus.
questions.keyConcept: Flocculonodular lobe controls vestibular function, balance, and eye movements via vestibular nuclei.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A lesion in the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) territory can result in which of the following neurological deficits?
options: Ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature of the body
questions.explanation: PICA supplies the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum. PICA syndrome causes ipsilateral dysphagia, hoarseness, decreased gag reflex (nucleus ambiguus), and cerebellar signs, with contralateral pain/temperature loss.
questions.keyConcept: PICA syndrome presents with ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits and contralateral sensory loss.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a function of the vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe)?
questions.explanation: The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) receives vestibular input and controls balance, posture, and eye movements, making it essential for spatial orientation.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibulocerebellum: controls balance and eye movements.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which function is primarily controlled by the primary motor cortex (area 4)?
options: Gives you the idea to move
questions.explanation: The primary motor cortex (area 4) controls discrete, fine voluntary movements, especially of the distal limbs. It contains large pyramidal neurons (Betz cells) in layer V.
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor cortex mediates fine, skilled voluntary movements via Betz cells and corticospinal output.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The spinal cord region that has the richest blood supply is:
questions.explanation: The cervical region of the spinal cord has the richest blood supply due to high metabolic demand and the watershed areas at C4-T1 levels, making it vulnerable to ischemic injury.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical cord has richest blood supply

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Occlusion of right anterior cerebral artery may lead to:
options: Paralysis of the left upper limb.
Paralysis of the left lower limb.
questions.explanation: Right anterior cerebral artery occlusion causes left lower limb paralysis (contralateral) since it supplies the medial motor cortex controlling the leg.
questions.keyConcept: Right ACA occlusion: left lower limb paralysis (contralateral).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The largest branch of the vertebral artery is:
questions.explanation: The largest branch of the vertebral artery is the basilar artery, formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction.
questions.keyConcept: Largest vertebral branch: basilar artery.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the spinal nerves, choose the CORRECT statement;
options: Its posterior root contains autonomic fibers.
Its ventral root carries a root ganglion.
The dendrites of its posterior root pass centrally.
Its autonomic fibers arise from anterior horn.
Cells of spinal ganglion are pseudounipolar.
questions.explanation: The autonomic fibers arise from the lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) of the spinal cord gray matter, not the anterior horn. The posterior root carries sensory fibers and contains the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral root carries motor fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Autonomic fibers arise from the lateral horn, not the anterior horn

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A protruded tongue which deviates to the right and shows wasting and fasciculations indicates a lesion in:
questions.explanation: Hypoglossal nerve palsy produces lower motor neuron signs in the tongue: the tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion when protruded, and there is wasting and fasciculations (spontaneous twitching of muscle fibers) on the affected side. This is because the genioglossus muscle on the affected side is weak and cannot push the tongue forward symmetrically. In contrast, upper motor neuron lesions produce tongue deviation away from the lesion side, without wasting or fasciculations.
questions.keyConcept: LMN hypoglossal lesion causes tongue deviation to the SAME side with wasting and fasciculations.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Loss of fine voluntary movements is most likely caused by a lesion in which area?
questions.explanation: Loss of fine voluntary movements (dexterity) indicates damage to the corticospinal tract or its origin in the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex), which mediates fractionated finger movements.
questions.keyConcept: Fine finger movements require intact corticospinal function at the precentral gyrus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Grey matter is .......... While white matter is ...........
questions.explanation: Grey matter (cell bodies) is centrally located in the spinal cord while white matter (myelinated fibers) is peripherally located, the reverse of the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Grey vs white matter distribution

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: ........... means sensation of movement, vibration, position
