questions.explanation: Proprioception encompasses the sensation of movement (kinesthesia), vibration, and joint/limb position, mediated by muscle spindles, tendon organs, and joint receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception definition

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All the following paired tract except:
questions.explanation: The sulcomarginal tract is a descending motor tract in the anterior column, not a paired bilateral tract like vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, and tectospinal.
questions.keyConcept: Unpaired tracts

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All those tract end in all level of spinal cord except:
questions.explanation: Rubrospinal and ventral vestibulospinal tracts do NOT extend to all spinal levels; lateral vestibulospinal, sulcomarginal, and reticulospinal do.
questions.keyConcept: Tract termination levels

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Molecular layer Contains all the following except:
options: Mossy fiber, dendrite of granular cell
questions.explanation: The molecular layer contains outer stellate cells, inner basket cells, Purkinje cell dendrites, Golgi cell dendrites, and parallel fibers (Granular cell axons); mossy fibers are in the granular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar molecular layer contents

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Large pyriform multipolar Cell:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are large pyriform (pear-shaped) multipolar neurons with a characteristic flask-shaped cell body and extensive dendritic tree.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje cell morphology

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: -- Contains T-shaped axon in Molecular layer:
questions.explanation: Granular cells have T-shaped axons (parallel fibers) that run tangentially in the molecular layer, forming excitatory synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites.
questions.keyConcept: Granular cell axon

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is/are true for central nervous system?
questions.explanation: Grey matter is central in spinal cord with neuron cell bodies; white matter is peripheral with myelinated fibers; the CNS lacks connective tissue framework.
questions.keyConcept: Grey white matter distribution

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the followings is not present in grey matter:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cell bodies, neuroglial cells, and unmyelinated fibers; myelinated nerve fibers are found in white matter.
questions.keyConcept: Grey matter composition

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following is a character of lumbar level of spinal cord?
options: Smallest white matter / grey matter ratio.
questions.explanation: Lumbar level has the smallest white matter/grey matter ratio because it has relatively less white matter (fewer descending motor fibers passing through).
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar spinal cord

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Anterior external arcuate fibres connect:
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers connect the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior external arcuate fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Posterior external arcuate fibres connect:
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Posterior external arcuate fibers connect the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior external arcuate fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following is true about climbing fibres:
options: Each fibre synapse with one Purkinje cell.
questions.explanation: Each climbing fiber forms powerful excitatory synapses with multiple Purkinje cell dendrites; one Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber.
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fiber Purkinje relationship

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which receptor has a motor efferent supply?
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles contain intrafusal fibers with gamma motor neuron innervation that adjusts sensitivity, unlike other receptors listed which are purely sensory.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle motor supply

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The Golgi tendon organ differs from the muscle spindle in that it:
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs lack gamma motor innervation (unlike muscle spindles), are in series with muscle, and detect tension; both have capsules.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon organ

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of the cervical level of the spinal cord?
options: Has the largest white matter/grey matter ratio
Contains the central canal in a ventral position
questions.explanation: The cervical spinal cord has the largest white matter-to-grey matter ratio among spinal cord levels because it contains the most descending and ascending fiber tracts connecting the brain to all body regions.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical cord has the largest white matter/grey matter ratio.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The first order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is located in:
questions.explanation: Proprioception from the lower body is carried by first-order neurons whose cell bodies are located in the spinal (dorsal root) ganglia, where peripheral receptors from muscle spindles and tendon organs synapse.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception first-order neuron: spinal (dorsal root) ganglia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a rapid, monosynaptic reflex that helps maintain muscle length?
questions.explanation: The stretch (myotatic) reflex is a monosynaptic reflex mediated by muscle spindles that detects changes in muscle length and rapidly adjusts muscle tone to maintain posture.
questions.keyConcept: Stretch reflex: monosynaptic reflex maintaining muscle length.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The muscle spindle is stretched by contraction of which fibres?
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal muscle fibers within the spindle, and when activated, they contract these fibers, stretching the sensory region and increasing spindle sensitivity to muscle stretch.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons stretch intrafusal fibers, increasing muscle spindle sensitivity.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Connects the vestibular nuclei with cranial nuclei of III, IV, & VI:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome includes: contralateral hemiparesis (pyramidal tract), contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue paralysis (hypoglossal nerve).
questions.keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome - contralateral weakness and proprioception loss

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following fibers carry proprioception from the upper limb to the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from the upper limb to the cerebellum. It originates from the accessory cuneate nucleus (lateral cuneate nucleus) and enters through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract carries upper limb proprioception

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following cerebellar parts has mainly spinal connections:
questions.explanation: The spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate zones) has mainly spinal connections - receives proprioceptive input from spine, controls axial and limb movement.选项B正确. The answer is B. Vestibulocerebellum has vestibular connections; cerebrocerebellum has cerebral connections.
questions.keyConcept: Spinocerebellum (vermis) has spinal connections - receives proprioceptive input, controls axial muscle tone.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure of the basal ganglia is classified as the paleostriatum?
questions.explanation: The globus pallidus internus (GPi) and externus (GPe) together form the paleostriatum (old striatum), while the putamen and caudate nucleus form the neostriatum (new striatum).
questions.keyConcept: Paleostriatum refers to the globus pallidus, distinguished from the neostriatum (caudate-putamen).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Purkinje cells are stimulated by the following except:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are excited by climbing fibers, mossy fibers (indirectly via granule cells), and parallel fibers; basket and Golgi cells provide inhibitory input.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje cell inputs

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding the cerebellum, choose one correct answer:
options: Middle cerebellar peduncle connects it to medulla oblongata.
Paleocerebellum is concerned with planning and programming movement.
questions.explanation: The spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate hemisphere) regulates muscle tone and coordination; the neocerebellum plans movement and the paleocerebellum controls equilibrium.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar functional divisions

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a function of the basal ganglia?
options: Modulation of movement and motor learning
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia modulate movement through indirect and direct pathways that influence thalamic output to the motor cortex, without directly executing voluntary movements.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia: modulate movement and motor learning, not direct execution.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Primary integrative neuron of cerebral Cortex:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are the primary integrative neurons of the cerebellar cortex, receiving input from climbing and parallel fibers and outputting via their axons to deep nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje cell function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Upper motor neuron lesion is characterized by:
options: Paralysis of muscle & all types of movement.
questions.explanation: Positive Babinski sign (dorsiflexion of big toe with fanning) is a hallmark of upper motor neuron lesion, indicating corticospinal tract damage and release of primitive reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Positive Babinski indicates UMN lesion

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Upper motor neuron lesion is characterized by
options: Plantar flexion of big toe on scratching skin of sole
questions.explanation: UMN lesion is characterized by spasticity (hypertonia), hyperreflexia, Babinski sign (plantar extension), and retained muscle bulk initially; option E (plantar flexion) describes normal reflex.
questions.keyConcept: UMN lesion characteristics

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Lower motor neuron lesion is characterized by
questions.explanation: LMN lesion is characterized by flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, muscle wasting, fasciculations, decreased/absent reflexes, and no Babinski sign (plantar reflex absent or normal flexion).
questions.keyConcept: LMN lesion characteristics

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an extrapyramidal tract?
questions.explanation: The corticospinal tract is the main pyramidal tract for voluntary movement. The reticulospinal, rubrospinal, and vestibulospinal tracts are extrapyramidal. The tectospinal tract is also extrapyramidal.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal tracts are the only major pyramidal motor pathways; all others are extrapyramidal.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The Charcot's artery is the largest branch of ……… set of central branches of circle of Willis.
questions.explanation: Charcot's artery (also called the artery of cerebral hemorrhage) is the largest anterolateral central branch of the circle of Willis, supplying the internal capsule and basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Charcot's artery: largest anterolateral central branch of circle of Willis.

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: The medial medullary syndrome includes:
options: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron lesion of XII.
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome includes: ipsilateral tongue paralysis (hypoglossal), contralateral hemiparesis (pyramidal), and contralateral loss of proprioception/fine touch (medial lemniscus). Pain and temperature are preserved.
questions.keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome includes tongue paralysis

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: Basal ganglia lesion may Not cause:
questions.explanation: Basal ganglia lesions cause rigidity, not flaccidity. Option E is correct. Flaccidity is a LMN sign or occurs with cerebellar lesions. Parkinsonian basal ganglia lesions produce cogwheel rigidity, not flaccidity. Options A-D are all recognized features of basal ganglia dysfunction: akinesia (inability to initiate movement), mask face (hypomimia), cogwheel rigidity, and monotonous speech.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia lesions produce extrapyramidal signs including rigidity and akinesia, not flaccidity.

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: A 42-year-old right-handed male arrives to the emergency department and is intoxicated. At the time of presentation, he is unable to move his hands and arms. The following day, once he is sober, a more thorough neurological examination reveals a complete flaccid paralysis of the upper limbs and severely diminished-to-absent reflex activity. What is the most likely area of spinal damage?
questions.explanation: This question appears to reference a spinal cord cross-section image showing different horn regions. Area C corresponds to the anterior horn where lower motor neurons reside. Damage to anterior horn cells at C8 level (or nearby) causes flaccid paralysis of the upper limbs with areflexia due to LMN destruction. This is consistent with anterior cord syndrome from watershed infarction, commonly seen after cardiac arrest or severe hypotension. The flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes indicate LMN, not UMN lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn cell damage causes flaccid paralysis with areflexia due to destruction of lower motor neurons.

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: Nicotine abuse may be managed by:
questions.explanation: Nicotine abuse can be managed with varenicline (partial nicotinic receptor agonist) and bupropion (norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor). However, the correct answer for 'management' includes both. Varenicline (A) is a partial agonist at alpha4-beta2 nicotinic receptors, reducing craving and withdrawal. Bupropion (B) increases dopamine, reducing craving. Buprenorphine (C) is for opioid dependence, not nicotine. Acamprosate (D) is for alcohol dependence. Option E likely represents 'both A and B'. The answer is E - both varenicline and bupropion are used for nicotine dependence.
questions.keyConcept: Nicotine dependence is managed with varenicline (partial nicotinic agonist) and bupropion (dopamine enhancer).

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: The following is a Wrong statement about Barbiturates
options: Dose dependent CNS depression up to coma
questions.explanation: Barbiturates are NOT strong enzyme inducers - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Barbiturates are potent CYP450 inducers, increasing metabolism of many drugs. Options A, C, D are correct: low therapeutic index, dose-dependent CNS depression, no specific antidote.
questions.keyConcept: Barbiturates are potent enzyme inducers that increase hepatic metabolism of many co-administered drugs.

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: Which of the following reversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes?
questions.explanation: Ibuprofen reversibly inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes, providing anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects. Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX; allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase (not COX); celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2; sulphinpyrazone inhibits COX but is a uricosuric.
questions.keyConcept: Ibuprofen as reversible non-selective COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: All of the following drugs have slower onset when taken intra‑muscular except:
questions.explanation: Midazolam has rapid IM onset due to high lipid solubility and small volume of distribution; benzodiazepines like lorazepam and alprazolam have slower IM absorption.
questions.keyConcept: Midazolam has faster IM onset than other benzodiazepines due to its pharmacokinetic profile.

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: An anxiolytic useful in a patient with a history of drug dependence is:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is preferred in patients with drug dependence history. Option A is correct. Buspirone has no abuse potential, no physical dependence, and can be used safely in patients with history of substance abuse. All other benzodiazepines (alprazolam, diazepam, lorazepam) have dependence liability.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone's lack of dependence makes it safe for patients with substance abuse history.

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: The following is a Wrong statement about BZDs
options: Lorazepam is an intermediate duration and effective anxiolytic and in status epilepticus
Midazolam is long acting acting used in anesthesia as hypnotic and should be avoided as anxiolytic
Alprazolam is effective in controlling the panic attacks
Diazepam is long acting & useful during alcohol withdrwal
questions.explanation: Midazolam is NOT long acting - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Midazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine used in anesthesia. Lorazepam is intermediate-acting (correct A). Alprazolam is effective for panic (correct C). Diazepam is long-acting for alcohol withdrawal (correct D).
questions.keyConcept: Midazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine used for induction of anesthesia and procedural sedation.

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: Buspirone is effective in case of:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is a 5‑HT1A partial agonist indicated specifically for generalized anxiety disorder; it has no efficacy for panic attacks (prefer benzodiazepines) or insomnia (prefer Z‑drugs).
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone is a first‑line treatment for generalized anxiety disorder but not for panic attacks or insomnia.

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: Which drug is used as a rescue medication in off akinesia?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine, a dopamine agonist, is used as rescue medication for off akinesia in Parkinson's disease due to its rapid onset when given subcutaneously.
questions.keyConcept: Off-akinesia management

questions.subject: clinical
questions.question: The following is a wrong statement about antiparkinsonian drugs
options: Selegiline is selective MAO-B inhibitor and decreases end of dose akinesia induced by L-dopa
Entacapone is selective COMT inhibitor and decreases of time of on/off effect of L dopa.
Amantadine increases dopamine release & blocks Glutamate (NMDA) receptors
Apomorphine taken orally to decrease off time & sudden akinetic episodes in advanced Parkinson’s disease
questions.explanation: Apomorphine is NOT taken orally - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Apomorphine is a D1/D2 agonist given by subcutaneous injection (not orally) for acute akinetic episodes in advanced Parkinson's. Selegiline is MAO-B inhibitor (correct). Entacapone is COMT inhibitor (correct). Amantadine increases dopamine release (correct).
questions.keyConcept: Apomorphine requires subcutaneous injection due to poor oral bioavailability and is used for acute rescue in advanced Parkinson's.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Medulloblastoma is a:
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a tumor of undifferentiated/primitive neuroectodermal cells (PNET), not a glial tumor (astrocytoma/oligodendroglioma) or neuronal tumor. It arises from cerebellar granule cell precursors.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma: tumor of undifferentiated cells (PNET), not glial or neuronal

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which statement is true regarding the layers of the cerebral cortex?
options: The outer band of Baillarger is present in the inner granular layer
The inner band of Baillarger is present in the molecular layer
The molecular layer contains large pyramidal cells
The inner granular layer lacks stellate cells
The multiform layer is the most superficial layer
questions.explanation: The outer band of Baillarger (optic radiation fibers) is found in the inner granular layer (layer IV) of the cerebral cortex, while the inner band is in layer V.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex layers

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following share in the cerebellar islands:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar islands (islands of granular cells) contain rosettes of mossy fiber terminals surrounded by dendrites of granule cells. Mossy fibers synapse with granule cell dendrites in these glomeruli.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar glomeruli: mossy fiber rosettes + granule cell dendrites; input from spinal cord/brainstem.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Climbing fibers:
questions.explanation: Climbing fibers are the axons of contralateral inferior olivary nucleus neurons. They ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle and climb on Purkinje cell dendrites. They carry error signals for motor learning. Mossy fibers (not climbing) end in granular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fibers: olivocerebellar (contralateral ION), climb on Purkinje dendrites, carry error signals.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which deficit is specifically associated with a lesion affecting climbing fibers of the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: Climbing fiber lesions specifically impair motor learning (adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex), as these fibers from the inferior olive encode error signals for cerebellar plasticity.
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fiber function

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: A major function of the climbing fibers to cerebellar cortex is:
questions.explanation: Climbing fiber function includes learning novel movement patterns. Option B is correct. Climbing fibers carry error signals and teach the cerebellum about unexpected events, contributing to motor learning ( cerebellar long-term depression). Option A is wrong (climbing fibers excite Purkinje cells, not inhibit). Option C is wrong (emotional stimuli are limbic, not cerebellar climbing fiber function). Option D is wrong (Purkinje cells, not climbing fibers, directly influence motor neurons via deep nuclei).
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fibers convey error signals to the cerebellum for motor learning and adaptation.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The inner band of baillarger is present in which layer
questions.explanation: The inner band of Baillarger is found in the INTERNAL PYRAMIDAL layer (layer V), which contains Betz cells in the motor cortex and other pyramidal neurons. The horizontal myelinated fibers form this band.
questions.keyConcept: Inner Baillarger: layer V (internal pyramidal) - contains Betz cells and corticospinal neurons.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Inner Pyramidal cells are present in layer …. of cerebral cortex:
questions.explanation: Inner pyramidal cells (also called Betz cells when giant) are found in layer V of the motor cortex, not in layers I-IV. Layer V is the internal pyramidal layer. The options I-IV are incorrect - inner pyramidal refers to layer V.
questions.keyConcept: Layer V (internal pyramidal): Betz cells, corticospinal neurons. Layer IV: thalamocortical input.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Giant cells of Betz are present in which layer of cerebral cortex:
questions.explanation: Giant cells of Betz are found in the INNER PYRAMIDAL layer (layer V) of the motor cortex. These are the largest neurons in the CNS and give rise to corticospinal tract fibers. They are characteristic of the primary motor area.
questions.keyConcept: Betz cells: giant pyramidal neurons in layer V of motor cortex; corticospinal tract origin.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Giant cells of Betz are present in which layer of cerebral cortex?
questions.explanation: Giant cells of Betz are large pyramidal neurons found in layer V (inner pyramidal layer) of the primary motor cortex. They give rise to the corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Giant cells of Betz in layer V (inner pyramidal) of primary motor cortex

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: All of the following are layers of cerebral cortex EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex has six layers: molecular (I), external granular (II), external pyramidal (III), internal granular (IV), internal pyramidal (V), and multiform (VI). The Purkinje layer is in the cerebellar cortex, not cerebral cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje layer is in cerebellum NOT cerebral cortex (cerebral has 6 layers, not Purkinje)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: As regards the histological structure of gray matter of spinal cord, choose the INCORRECT statement:
options: It contain nerve cells & neuroglia cells.
The nerve fibers within the gray matter are mostly myelinated.
Golgi type II neurons terminate in gray matter near their origin.
Golgi type I neurons form long ascending fibers.
questions.explanation: Nerve fibers within the gray matter are mostly unmyelinated or thinly myelinated, not heavily myelinated. Heavy myelination is characteristic of white matter tracts. The gray matter contains neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and glial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Gray matter fibers are mostly unmyelinated; white matter fibers are myelinated

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: All about muscle spindle true except:
options: Present in parallel with sk. Muscle fibers.
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles contain intrafusal muscle fibers (not collagen fibers primarily). The capsule encloses the spindle but the internal structure is muscle fiber-based. They are in parallel with extrafusal fibers, have gamma efferents, and are encapsulated.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle: parallel with extrafusal fibers, contains intrafusal muscle fibers, encapsulated, gamma innervation.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of muscle spindle:
options: Present In series with muscle fibers.
Innervated by afferent & efferent nerve fiber.
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles are innervated by both afferent (Ia, II) and efferent (gamma) nerve fibers. They contain intrafusal muscle fibers (not collagen), are in parallel with extrafusal fibers, respond to stretch, and are encapsulated.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle: parallel arrangement, intrafusal fibers, afferent + efferent innervation, stretch receptor.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: One of the following is a character of lumbar level of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The lumbar spinal cord has the smallest white matter/grey matter ratio because it contains a large amount of grey matter (lower motor neurons for legs) relative to white matter (mostly descending tracts passing through). It has lateral horns for sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar cord: large grey matter (LMN for lower limb), small white/grey ratio, lateral horns present.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question:
Which of the following is/are true for central nervous system?
I. It is rich in connective tissue cells.
II. It is soft jelly like.
III. It has grey matter and white matter.
questions.explanation: CNS is NOT rich in connective tissue - it is poor in CT, derived mainly from neuroectoderm. It IS soft and jelly-like (due to high water content), and has grey and white matter.
questions.keyConcept: CNS: poor in CT, soft/jelly-like (high water), has grey (neurons) and white (myelinated) matter.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The processes of protoplasmic astrocytes characterized by:
questions.explanation: Protoplasmic astrocytes (in grey matter) have numerous short branching processes. Fibrous astrocytes (in white matter) have few long unbranched processes. Both types express GFAP and have foot processes on blood vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Protoplasmic astrocytes: grey matter, numerous short processes. Fibrous astrocytes: white matter, few long processes.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Accessory cuneate nucleus give rise to:
questions.explanation: The accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus gives rise to UNCROSSED fibers that ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to reach the cerebellum (cuneocerebellar tract). These carry proprioception from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus: uncrossed fibers → cerebellum via ICP; proprioception from upper limb.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the grey matter?
options: It is located outside the white matter in spinal cord.
It is formed of nerve cells mainly.
It has satellite cells sheath around its cells.
questions.explanation: Grey matter in the spinal cord is located centrally (not outside white matter), composed mainly of nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers. It is surrounded by white matter and contains neuroglia.
questions.keyConcept: Grey matter is centrally located, formed mainly of nerve cells (not outside white matter)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in:
options: Arcuate nucleus of the same side.
Arcuate nucleus of the opposite side.
questions.explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers (from the inferior olivary nucleus) relay to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. They carry information that has already decussated at the level of the inferior olivary nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in the inferior olivary nucleus

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which type of neuron forms synaptic junctions with intrafusal muscle fibers within a muscle spindle?
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal muscle fibers within muscle spindles, regulating spindle sensitivity and the stretch reflex loop.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The processes of protoplasmic astrocytes are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Protoplasmic astrocytes (found in grey matter) have numerous short, branching processes. Fibrous astrocytes (found in white matter) have few long, thin processes.
questions.keyConcept: Protoplasmic astrocytes: numerous short branching processes (grey matter)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Inner pyramidal cells are present in layer .... of cerebral cortex:
questions.explanation: Inner pyramidal cells (also called giant pyramidal cells or Betz cells in motor cortex) are found in layer V of the cerebral cortex. They give rise to corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inner pyramidal cells in layer V of cerebral cortex (corticospinal origin)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Cerebellar glomeruli contain the following structures EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar glomeruli contain rosettes of mossy fibers, dendrites of granule cells, and axons of Golgi cells (inhibitory). They do NOT contain dendrites of basket cells - those are involved in different synapses on Purkinje cell bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar glomerulus: mossy fiber rosette + granule cell dendrites + Golgi cell axons. Basket cells synapse on Purkinje soma.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The main efferent fiber of the cerebellar cortex is formed by axons of:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are the SOLE OUTPUT of the cerebellar cortex - their axons are the only fibers leaving the cortex to deeper nuclei. These axons are inhibitory (GABAergic). Golgi, basket, and granule cells are all interneurons.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje cells: only efferent of cerebellar cortex; GABAergic; projects to deep nuclei and vestibular nuclei.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The molecular layer of cerebellum contains which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: The molecular layer of cerebellum contains stellate cells (with cell bodies here), basket cells (with cell bodies here), and the dendrites of Purkinje cells and Golgi cells. Purkinje cell bodies are in the Purkinje layer. Golgi cell bodies are in the granular layer. Cerebellar glomeruli are in the granular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar molecular layer: stellate + basket cells, Purkinje/Golgi dendrites. Purkinje layer: Purkinje cell bodies. Granular layer: granule cells, Golgi bodies, glomeruli.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The deepest layer of the cerebellar cortex is
questions.explanation: The cerebellar cortex has 3 layers: molecular layer (outer), Purkinje cell layer (middle), and granular layer (deepest/innermost). The granular layer contains granule cells, Golgi cells, and cerebellar glomeruli.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar cortex layers (superficial to deep): molecular → Purkinje → granular.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Parallel fibers make synapse with Purkinje cells dendrites:
questions.explanation: Parallel fibers (axons of granule cells) make basket-like synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites in the molecular layer. These are excitatory synapses using glutamate as neurotransmitter.
questions.keyConcept: Parallel fibers make basket-like synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: A 5-year-old child suffered from headache & blurring of vision. Radiological examination showed a cerebellar tumor. Microscopic examination of a biopsy from this tumor revealed diffuse infiltration by malignant small round cells with rosette formation. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma presents in children with cerebellar symptoms (ataxia, increased ICP) and shows malignant small round cells with rosette formation (Homer-Wright rosettes). It is a WHO grade IV PNET.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma: small round cells, rosette formation, cerebellar tumor in children

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: All of the following are histological layers of the cerebral cortex except:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are characteristic of the CEREBELLAR cortex, not cerebral cortex. The cerebral cortex has 6 layers: molecular, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, internal pyramidal, and multiform. The cerebellar cortex has 3 layers.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex layers: I-VI (6 layers). Cerebellar cortex: molecular, Purkinje, granular (3 layers).

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of cervical level of spinal cord?
options: Has largest white matter/grey matter ratio.
questions.explanation: Cervical spinal cord has the largest white matter/grey matter ratio because it contains the most descending and ascending fibers passing to/from the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical spinal cord

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The following statement is wrong
options: Chronic anxiety is added to antidepressant in the beginning of therapy till the effect of antidepressant appears
Chronic insomnia should be treatment with antidepressant such as mirtazapine
Short acting BDZs are preferred in insomnia with difficulty in falling asleep
Panic disorders require highly potent drugs such as alprazolam & buspirone
Dose adjustment for most of BDZs is required in hepatic impairment
questions.explanation: Panic disorders do NOT require highly potent drugs such as alprazolam AND buspirone - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Alprazolam is highly potent and effective for panic; buspirone is NOT effective for acute panic attacks. SSRIs are first-line for panic disorder. Option E about hepatic impairment is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Panic disorder is treated with SSRIs or high-potency benzodiazepines (alprazolam); buspirone is ineffective for panic.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: What are the key microscopic features of oligodendrogliomas WHO grade III?
options: More aggressive with higher cell density, nuclear anaplasia, and prominent mitotic activity
Low cellularity with mild nuclear atypia
questions.explanation: Anaplastic oligodendroglioma (WHO grade III) shows: increased cellularity, marked nuclear atypia, brisk mitotic activity, and microvascular proliferation. Unlike grade II, grade III shows clear malignant features. The 'fried egg' appearance may still be present but with more pleomorphism.选项A符合WHO III级标准. Options B, C, D describe features of other tumors (higher grade astrocytoma or pilocytic astrocytoma). The answer is A. Grade III oligodendrogliomas have 1p/19q codeletion and respond well to chemotherapy.
questions.keyConcept: Anaplastic oligodendroglioma (grade III) shows marked nuclear atypia and mitotic activity, distinguishing it from grade II.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: A 10‑year‑old girl has a cystic cerebellar tumour. Microscopy shows spindle cells with hair‑like processes, microcysts, and Rosenthal fibres. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma in children shows characteristic hair-like processes (ROSE), microcysts, and Rosenthal fibers; often cystic with mural nodule.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: Psammoma bodies are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concretions) are characteristic of meningiomas, papillary thyroid carcinoma, and serous cystadenocarcinoma of ovary.
questions.keyConcept: Psammoma bodies characteristic of meningioma (and some carcinomas)

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: Microscopic rosette formation is a characteristic feature of:
questions.explanation: Rosette formation (Homer-Wright rosettes) is characteristic of medulloblastoma and other primitive neuroectodermal tumors (PNETs).
questions.keyConcept: Rosette formation characteristic of medulloblastoma (PNET)

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: Oligodendroglioma is not a:
questions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas are low-grade (grade II) tumors, not high-grade. They are glial tumors, cerebral tumors, and well-circumscribed. High-grade would be anaplastic oligodendroglioma (grade III).
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendroglioma is a low-grade tumor, NOT high-grade - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is a WHO grade IV tumor?
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a WHO grade IV tumor (most malignant), occurring in the cerebellum, especially in children. It is a small round blue cell tumor with high mitotic activity and can metastasize via CSF.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma is WHO grade IV malignant cerebellar tumor

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: A 33-year-old male presents with seizures, MRI shows an ill-defined area of infiltrative tumor expanding the frontal lobe. Biopsy of this lesion shows glial tissue with slightly increased cellularity and mild nuclear pleomorphism. No mitotic activity, no necrosis & no vascular proliferation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Grade II astrocytomas show increased cellularity, mild nuclear pleomorphism, but no mitotic activity, necrosis, or vascular proliferation. They are diffuse astrocytomas in young adults, slower growing than anaplastic or GBM.
questions.keyConcept: Grade II astrocytoma: slightly increased cellularity, mild pleomorphism, no necrosis/mitosis

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: A 5‑year‑old boy has recent‑onset gait instability and ataxia. MRI shows a midline posterior fossa mass. Biopsy reveals sheets of primitive small round cells with many mitoses. Which cytogenetic abnormality is most common?
options: Loss of the short arm of chromosome 17 (17p)
Loss of the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q)
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma shows loss of chromosome 17p; it's a small round blue cell tumor of the posterior fossa in children.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma genetics

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: A 32‑year‑old woman has right arm weakness and reduced light touch on the left leg. CSF shows oligoclonal bands. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis presents with oligoclonal bands in CSF, periventricular white matter lesions, and relapsing-remitting neurological deficits.
questions.keyConcept: Multiple sclerosis diagnosis

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: Which of the following tumors is a WHO grade IV:
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a WHO grade IV tumor (most malignant). It arises in the cerebellum, more common in children. Diffuse astrocytoma (grade II-III) and oligodendroglioma (grade II-III) are slower-growing tumors. Ependymoma is grade II-III. WHO grading: Grade I (pilocytic astrocytoma - benign), Grade II (low-grade), Grade III (anaplastic), Grade IV (most aggressive - medulloblastoma, glioblastoma). Medulloblastoma is highly cellular, mitotically active, and has the worst prognosis among primary brain tumors in children, requiring aggressive treatment.
questions.keyConcept: WHO grade IV brain tumors (medulloblastoma) are the most malignant, distinguishing from grade II-III tumors.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: Pilocytic astrocytoma is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a WHO grade I tumor (benign) with good prognosis. Characteristic features: occurs in children (most common pediatric brain tumor), commonly arises in cerebellum (though can occur elsewhere), often cystic with a mural nodule. Option D states 'bad prognosis' which is INCORRECT - pilocytic astrocytoma has excellent prognosis with complete surgical resection (5-year survival >90%). This is the EXCEPT question, so D is the answer. In contrast, diffuse astrocytoma (grade II) and anaplastic astrocytoma (grade III) have progressively worse prognoses.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a benign childhood cerebellar tumor with excellent prognosis after complete resection.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: The most common brain tumor in children:
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children, occurring in the cerebellum. It is a PNET (primitive neuroectodermal tumor) with small round blue cells.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma is most common malignant brain tumor in children

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: A male patient 40 years old presented with hemiplegia & deafness. Radiological examination showed a tumor at the cerebellopontine angle. Biopsy from this tumor showed a neurogenic tumor formed of hypercellular and hypocellular areas. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Schwannomas (neurilemmomas) at the cerebellopontine angle show hypercellular (Antoni A) and hypocellular (Antoni B) areas. They arise from Schwann cells.
questions.keyConcept: Schwannoma: Antoni A and B areas, hypercellular/hypocellular, cerebellopontine angle

questions.subject: pathology
questions.question: A male patient 40 years presented with left-sided hemiplegia, brain MRI revealed a space-occupying lesion in the right cerebral hemisphere. Biopsy examination showed a highly cellular tumor with malignant cells, areas of necrosis & vascular proliferation. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme shows highly cellular tumor with malignant cells, necrosis, and vascular proliferation. These features distinguish it from anaplastic astrocytoma (which lacks necrosis) and ependymoma.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma: necrosis and vascular proliferation = hallmark features

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The main benefit of adding carbidopa to levodopa in Sinemet is that carbidopa:
options: Inhibits peripheral aromatic L‑amino acid decarboxylase
questions.explanation: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, preventing peripheral levodopa conversion and increasing CNS availability.
questions.keyConcept: Carbidopa mechanism

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: To increase the synthesis of catecholamines in the brain, a patient with Parkinsonism may be given
questions.explanation: L-dopa (levodopa) is the direct precursor of dopamine and is administered to increase catecholamine synthesis in Parkinson's disease, where dopaminergic neurons have degenerated. L-dopa crosses the blood-brain barrier unlike dopamine itself, then is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase.
questions.keyConcept: L-dopa as dopamine precursor in Parkinson's disease treatment

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which antiviral drug is used to treat neonates with herpes simplex virus encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Acyclovir (guanine analog) is the treatment of choice for HSV encephalitis in neonates, reducing mortality when given early.
questions.keyConcept: HSV encephalitis treatment

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Slow pain:
options: Is carried along type A-delta fibers.
Pathway activates the non-specific thalamic nuclei.
Is perceived mainly in sensory cortex.
questions.explanation: Slow pain is transmitted by unmyelinated C fibers to non-specific thalamic nuclei, perceived diffusely in the sensory cortex, and produces dull, poorly localized, prolonged pain.
questions.keyConcept: Slow pain: C fibers, non-specific thalamic nuclei, diffuse perception.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: A drug inducing a GABA- mediated sedative hypnotic effect in intensive care units
questions.explanation: Propofol induces GABA-mediated sedation in ICU. Option B is correct. Propofol enhances GABA-A receptor activity, providing sedation. Ketamine (C) acts on NMDA receptors. Fentanyl (A) is opioid. Propofol is preferred for ICU sedation due to rapid onset/offset and easy titration.
questions.keyConcept: Propofol provides GABAergic sedation with rapid onset and recovery, ideal for ICU sedation protocols.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following concerning Naloxone is not correct:
options: Has a shorter half-life than its agonist
Given in anesthesia to reverse CNS depression of its agonist
It’s a specific antagonist to opioid receptors
questions.explanation: Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist at mu, kappa, and delta receptors. Properties: 1) Shorter half-life (~1 hour) than most opioid agonists (like morphine, heroin) - this is why repeated dosing may be needed; 2) Given parenterally (IV, IM, SC), NOT orally - oral bioavailability is poor due to first-pass metabolism; 3) Used to reverse opioid overdose (respiratory depression, CNS depression); 4) Specific antagonist at opioid receptors. Option B is NOT correct because naloxone is NOT given orally (this is the incorrect statement). The correct answer is B.
questions.keyConcept: Naloxone is a short-acting opioid antagonist given parenterally (not orally) to reverse opioid overdose.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following abused drug is wrongly matched to replacement therapy:
questions.explanation: Disulfiram is used to treat alcohol dependence - it inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing accumulation of acetaldehyde when alcohol is consumed. However, this is a form of aversion therapy, not replacement therapy. Replacement therapy involves substituting a safer alternative. The WRONG pairing is C - Disulfiram is NOT replacement therapy. Pentobarbital/phenobarbital (A) - barbiturate replacement for barbiturate dependence; Morphine/methadone (B) - opioid replacement; Alprazolam/diazepam (D) - benzodiazepine replacement (longer-acting for shorter-acting). Disulfiram works through psychological deterrence, not replacement. The answer is C - alcohol/disulfiram is incorrectly matched to replacement therapy.
questions.keyConcept: Disulfiram is aversion therapy for alcohol, not replacement therapy like methadone for opioids.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: What is the classification of codeine? And what’s it’s uses?
questions.explanation: Codeine is classified as a weak opioid agonist with moderate analgesic and antitussive effects. Uses: mild-moderate pain (often with acetaminophen or aspirin), cough suppression, and diarrhea treatment.选项A正确. The answer is A. Codeine's analgesic effect requires metabolic conversion to morphine by CYP2D6.
questions.keyConcept: Codeine is a weak opioid used for mild pain, cough, and diarrhea - requires CYP2D6 activation to morphine.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not common between pethidine & tramadol
options: Increase risk of convulsions with high doses
questions.explanation: Pethidine and tramadol both have analgesic properties and can cause seizures at high doses, but tramadol's action is only partially reversed by naloxone (has non-opioid mechanisms), unlike pethidine.
questions.keyConcept: Tramadol vs pethidine naloxone reversal

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which drug can be used to manage fentanyl intoxication?
questions.explanation: Naloxone, like naltrexone, is an opioid antagonist that can reverse fentanyl intoxication by competitively blocking opioid receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Fentanyl intoxication treatment

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which correctly describes the difference between tramadol and morphine?
options: Tramadol is a mixed opioid–nonopioid analgesic that increases serotonin and norepinephrine, while morphine is a pure opioid agonist
Tramadol is a pure opioid agonist, morphine is mixed
Both act only on μ receptors
Morphine increases serotonin and norepinephrine, tramadol does not
Tramadol has no effect on opioid receptors
questions.explanation: Tramadol is a mixed mechanism analgesic with both mu-opioid agonist activity and inhibition of serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake, unlike pure morphine.
questions.keyConcept: Tramadol vs morphine

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following opioid drug should be avoided in patient taking MAOI:
questions.explanation: Meperidine (pethidine) should be avoided with MAOIs due to risk of serotonin syndrome and severe adverse reactions. It has serotonergic properties unlike other opioids. Morphine, fentanyl, and codeine do not have this specific interaction.
questions.keyConcept: Meperidine contraindicated with MAOIs (serotonin syndrome risk)

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following analgesic is not recommended to be taken in renal failure or more than 48 hours for fear of convulsions:
questions.explanation: Meperidine (pethidine) should be avoided in renal failure and not used for more than 48 hours due to accumulation of normeperidine, which causes seizures. Morphine, codeine, and tramadol are safer alternatives.
questions.keyConcept: Meperidine contraindicated in renal failure (normeperidine accumulation causes seizures)

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not an adverse effect of direct D2 receptor agonists
questions.explanation: Insomnia is NOT an adverse effect of direct D2 receptor agonists. Option C is correct. D2 agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) commonly cause hallucinations, dyskinesia (especially with long-term use), and impulse control disorders. Insomnia is not a typical adverse effect; actually, these drugs can cause daytime sleepiness. Amantadine is known to cause insomnia.
questions.keyConcept: D2 agonists cause neuropsychiatric effects (hallucinations, dyskinesia, impulse control disorders) but not insomnia.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not an adverse effect of amantadine
questions.explanation: Daytime sleepiness is NOT an adverse effect of amantadine. Option B is correct. Amantadine causes hallucinations, livedo reticularis (skin rash), ankle edema, and tolerance. Insomnia is actually a known amantadine effect (along with dizziness). Daytime sleepiness is more typical of dopamine agonists.
questions.keyConcept: Amantadine commonly causes insomnia, livedo reticularis, and ankle edema, but not daytime sleepiness.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Addition of carbidopa to L dopa increases risk of all the following adverse effects except
questions.explanation: Nausea & vomiting is NOT increased by adding carbidopa. Option C is correct. Carbidopa prevents peripheral conversion of L-dopa to dopamine, reducing peripheral side effects including nausea/vomiting. However, it increases brain dopamine, which can increase CNS adverse effects: dyskinesia, hallucinations, and confusion.
questions.keyConcept: Carbidopa reduces peripheral L-dopa side effects (nausea) but increases central dopaminergic effects (dyskinesia, hallucinations).

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not correctly matched to its use:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is used for generalized anxiety disorder but lacks efficacy for panic attacks. Panic attacks are typically treated with SSRIs, benzodiazepines, or CBT.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone is a selective anxiolytic for generalized anxiety but lacks efficacy for panic attacks.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The major limitation to the use of benzodiazepines in anxiety is:
options: No antidote is available if overdose toxicity occurs.
questions.explanation: Dependence is the major limitation to benzodiazepine use. Option C is correct. Benzodiazepines cause physical and psychological dependence with chronic use, limiting their long-term use. Options A, B, D are less accurate: flumazenil is an antidote (A is wrong), cardiovascular depression is rare (B), and respiratory depression is mainly with high doses or combined with other depressants (D).
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepine dependence is the primary clinical limitation, requiring careful prescribing and monitoring.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The dose of benzodiazepines should be adjusted in:
questions.explanation: Dose adjustment is needed in elderly AND with alcohol AND with hepatic dysfunction. Option D is correct. All three factors require dose adjustment: elderly have reduced metabolism, alcohol potentiates CNS depression, hepatic dysfunction impairs metabolism of benzodiazepines.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepine dosing requires adjustment in elderly, hepatic impairment, and when combined with CNS depressants.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Flumazenil is an antidote for all the following Except:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is NOT reversed by flumazenil. Option B is correct. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist. Triazolam (A), zolpidem (C), and diazepam (D) are all benzodiazepine-related drugs reversed by flumazenil. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A agonist anxiolytic that does not act on benzodiazepine receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil only reverses benzodiazepines and zolpidem; it does not reverse buspirone (5-HT1A agonist) or barbiturates.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: All the following characteristics are shared by flumazenil and naloxone Except:
options: Have shorter t1/2 than their respective agonists.
Given in anesthesia to reverse CNS depression of their agonists.
Specific respiratory stimulants in benzodiazepine or opioid toxicity.
questions.explanation: Flumazenil and naloxone are NOT given orally - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Both flumazenil and naloxone are given parenterally (IV), not orally, because they have poor oral bioavailability and rapid first-pass metabolism. Options A, C, D are correct shared characteristics.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil and naloxone require parenteral administration due to poor oral bioavailability and rapid hepatic metabolism.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Abuse potential of buspirone is low because
options: It has a weak anxiolytic effect
It has no recognizable effect on brain neurotransmitters.
It has a delayed onset of action.
Its marked sedating effect is troublesome.
questions.explanation: Buspirone has delayed onset of action - this explains low abuse potential. Option C is correct. Unlike benzodiazepines which act immediately, buspirone takes 2-4 weeks for anxiolytic effect. This delayed onset, combined with lack of sedation and no GABA activity, results in low abuse potential.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone's delayed onset of action contributes to its minimal abuse potential compared to benzodiazepines.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following anxiolytic drug do not act through GABA
questions.explanation: Buspirone does not act through GABA. Option B is correct. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist anxiolytic. Zolpidem (A), lorazepam (C), and phenobarbital (D) all enhance GABAergic transmission. Buspirone works through serotonin modulation.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A serotonin receptor partial agonist, distinct from GABA-acting anxiolytics.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following drug has no sedative hypnotic effect
questions.explanation: Flumazenil has no sedative hypnotic effect. Option C is correct. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist that blocks GABA-benzodiazepine receptors. It reverses sedation and would not cause sedation. Antihistamines (A), tricyclics (B), and clonidine (D) all have sedative effects.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist with no intrinsic sedative activity.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is wrong about zolpidem
options: Less hangover and rebound insomnia than BDZ
Its toxicity can be reversed by flumazenil
Tolerance & dependence is more common than BDZs
questions.explanation: Tolerance and dependence is LESS common with zolpidem than BZDs - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Zolpidem actually has LESS dependence potential than benzodiazepines. Options A, B, C are correct: zolpidem is short-acting non-BZD, has less hangover/rebound, and toxicity is reversed by flumazenil.
questions.keyConcept: Zolpidem has lower dependence potential than benzodiazepines despite being a GABA-A receptor modulator.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Dentists avoid extraction in infection because of all the following Except:
options: Infection decreases extracellular unionized form of local anesthetics.
Infection reduces crossing of local anesthetics inside nerve cell.
Infection increases extracellular unionized form of local anesthetics.
questions.explanation: Infection's acidic environment (low pH) DECREASES the unionized (active) fraction of local anesthetics, reducing their efficacy.
questions.keyConcept: Infection's acidic environment reduces local anesthetic efficacy by decreasing the unionized (nerve-penetrating) form.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not true about cocaine:
options: Acute toxicity may result in convulsions.
questions.explanation: Cocaine is a potent VASOCONSTRICTOR, not vasodilator. Option C is incorrect. Cocaine blocks norepinephrine reuptake, causing vasoconstriction and hypertension. This is why it causes local anesthesia without needing epinephrine. Options A, B, D are correct: cocaine is a local anesthetic, can cause convulsions, and chronic use causes psychosis.
questions.keyConcept: Cocaine's vasoconstrictor properties (from norepinephrine reuptake inhibition) distinguish it from other local anesthetics.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not adverse effect of halothane
questions.explanation: Halothane causes hypotension, not hypertension. Option C is incorrect. Halothane causes cardiovascular depression: bradycardia, hypotension, and arrhythmias. It also causes malignant hyperthermia, hepatic toxicity, and increases ICP. The vasodilation and myocardial depression lead to hypotension.
questions.keyConcept: Halothane's cardiovascular effects include bradycardia, hypotension, and arrhythmias due to myocardial depression.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Nitrous oxide, the following is incorrect
options: Safer than halothane with less respiratory depression and less hepatic toxicity
Risk of abuse on prolonged exposure
Iron deficiency anemia on chronic exposure
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide does NOT cause iron deficiency anemia - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Nitrous oxide inactivates vitamin B12, causing megaloblastic anemia (not iron deficiency). Options A, B, C are correct: N2O is weak analgesic, safer than halothane, and causes abuse with prolonged exposure.
questions.keyConcept: Nitrous oxide causes B12 inactivation and megaloblastic anemia with chronic use, not iron deficiency.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not common adverse effect of nitrous oxide
options: Hypoxia if take pure without oxygen
Increase pressure in the middle ear
questions.explanation: Hepatic toxicity is NOT a common adverse effect of nitrous oxide. Option D is correct. N2O is minimally metabolized and has excellent safety profile. Hypoxia (A), middle ear pressure (B), and abortion risk (C) are documented concerns. Unlike halothane, N2O rarely causes hepatotoxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Nitrous oxide has minimal hepatic toxicity unlike halogenated anesthetics.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following is a wrong statement?
options: Propranolol decrease metabolism of lidocaine and may precipitate its toxicity
Addition of epinephrine to local anesthetics may induce severe hypertension due to unopposed alpha action
Lidocaine with epinephrine should be avoided in patient taking antidepressant drugs such as TCA & MAOIs
Felypressin is not suitable with local anesthetics in cardiac patients
questions.explanation: Felypressin IS suitable with local anesthetics in cardiac patients - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Felypressin (vasopressin analog) is preferred over epinephrine in cardiac patients because it has less cardiac effects. Option A, B, C are correct: propranolol decreases lidocaine metabolism, epinephrine with alpha unopposed action causes hypertension, TCA/MAOI combo with epinephrine risks hypertensive crisis.
questions.keyConcept: Felypressin is the vasoconstrictor of choice in cardiac patients due to minimal cardiac stimulation.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not correctly matched to its mechanism of action:
questions.explanation: Clonazepam acts through GABA enhancement, not Cl- channel blockade - this is NOT correctly matched. Option B is incorrect. Clonazepam (benzodiazepine) enhances GABA-A receptor activity, increasing chloride channel opening frequency. Sodium channel blockade (A) is phenytoin. GABA transaminase inhibition (C) is valproate. T-channel blockade (D) is ethosuximide.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepines enhance GABAergic inhibition by increasing chloride channel opening frequency.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Ethosuximide useful in
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide is useful in absence seizure. Option B is correct. Ethosuximide is first-line for childhood absence epilepsy. It does not work for partial epilepsy (A) or tonic-clonic seizures (C). Valproate would cover both absence and tonic-clonic.
questions.keyConcept: Ethosuximide's specificity for absence seizures comes from thalamic T-channel modulation.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following is not adverse effect of phenytoin?
questions.explanation: Agranulocytosis is NOT a phenytoin adverse effect. Option C is correct. Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia, osteomalacia (via vitamin D metabolism), and teratogenicity (fetal hydantoin syndrome). Agranulocytosis is more associated with carbamazepine. Phenytoin's hematologic effects include macrocytosis and megaloblastic anemia (not agranulocytosis).
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin's adverse effects include gingival hyperplasia, osteomalacia, and teratogenicity; agranulocytosis is rare.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following antiepilpetic drug is not enzyme inducer
questions.explanation: Valproate is NOT an enzyme inducer. Option C is correct. Valproate is an enzyme inhibitor, not inducer. Phenytoin (A), carbamazepine (B), and phenobarbital (D) are all potent CYP450 inducers that increase metabolism of many drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate inhibits hepatic enzymes, unlike phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital which are inducers.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Regarding adverse effects & precautions with sumatriptan, which is incorrect?
options: Contraindicated in aptients with ischemic heart disease
questions.explanation: Sumatriptan causes hypertension, not hypotension. Option C is incorrect. Sumatriptan (5-HT1B/1D agonist) causes coronary vasoconstriction and can raise blood pressure. Options A, B, D, E are correct: bad taste, chest pressure, serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, contraindicated in IHD.
questions.keyConcept: Sumatriptan's vasoconstrictor effects can cause hypertension and chest pressure; it's contraindicated in IHD.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Regarding adverse effects of ergotamine, which is incorrect?
options: Vasospasm & gangrene . Avoided in peripheral vascular disease
Valvular heart disease with long term use
questions.explanation: Ergotamine does NOT cause hypotension. Option E is incorrect. Ergotamine causes vasoconstriction (leading to hypertension, not hypotension), nausea/vomiting, chest pressure, and with long-term use can cause valvular heart disease and peripheral vasospasm/gangrene.
questions.keyConcept: Ergotamine's vasoconstrictor properties cause hypertension and risk of gangrene, not hypotension.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following drug is contraindicated during acute attack of migraine
questions.explanation: Dihydroergotamine is contraindicated during acute migraine attack (with propranolol). Option D is incorrect. Dihydroergotamine is used FOR acute attacks (not prevented). Propranolol, amitriptyline, and valproate are prophylactic agents. Combining DHE with propranolol risks hypertension due to additive vasoconstriction.
questions.keyConcept: Dihydroergotamine is a migraine abortive agent; propranolol prophylaxis combined with it risks hypertension.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Fluoxetine does not induce:
options: Serotonin syndrome if co- administered with tranylcypromine
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine does not induce marked sedation. Option D is correct. Fluoxetine is an SSRI that causes stimulation/anxiety, not sedation. It can cause nausea and anxiety. Sedation is more associated with other antidepressants (TCAs, mirtazapine). SSRIs combined with MAOIs (tranylcypromine) can cause serotonin syndrome (A is correct).
questions.keyConcept: Fluoxetine causes activating side effects (nausea, anxiety, insomnia) rather than sedation.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following concerning venlafaxine is not true:
options: Anticholinergic side effects are frequently encountered with its use.
It is a norepinephrine serotonin reuptake inhibitor.
Nausea is a troublesome side effect.
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine does NOT have frequent anticholinergic effects. Option A is incorrect. Venlafaxine (SNRI) has minimal anticholinergic activity. Nausea (C) is common, hypertension (D) can occur. It inhibits norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake (B is correct). Anticholinergic effects are characteristic of TCAs, not SNRIs.
questions.keyConcept: SNRIs like venlafaxine have minimal anticholinergic effects, unlike tricyclic antidepressants.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Severe hypertension is most likely to occur following intake of old cheese with
questions.explanation: Tranylcypromine causes severe hypertensive crisis with tyramine (old cheese). Option A is correct. Tranylcypromine is a non-selective MAOI; tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, wine, fermented foods) cause hypertensive crisis. Moclobemide (B) and selegiline (C) are selective MAO-B inhibitors with less food interaction. Bupropion (D) has no MAOI activity.
questions.keyConcept: Non-selective MAOIs like tranylcypromine require tyramine-restricted diet to prevent hypertensive crisis.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Nocturnal enuresis is treated with imipramine but not fluoxetine because
options: Imipramine induces insomnia while fluoxetine induces sedation.
Imipramine possess anticholinergic effect but fluoxetine does not.
questions.explanation: Imipramine has anticholinergic effect (treats enuresis); fluoxetine does not. Option C is correct. Nocturnal enuresis is treated with imipramine's anticholinergic effect (reduces bladder contractions). Fluoxetine has no anticholinergic activity. Both can cause insomnia (A is wrong), and imipramine is not necessarily safer than fluoxetine.
questions.keyConcept: Imipramine's anticholinergic effect reduces detrusor muscle activity, treating enuresis; fluoxetine lacks this mechanism.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Reduction in sexual function is least seen with
questions.explanation: Bupropion has LEAST sexual dysfunction. Option C is correct. Bupropion (NDRI) has minimal sexual side effects compared to SSRIs (fluoxetine) and TCAs (imipramine). This makes it useful when sexual dysfunction is a concern. Mirtazapine (B) also has lower sexual dysfunction than SSRIs.
questions.keyConcept: Bupropion's dopaminergic mechanism avoids the sexual dysfunction common with serotonergic antidepressants.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not correctly matched:
options: Moclobemide/ selective monoamine oxidase - B inhibitor.
questions.explanation: Moclobemide is a selective MAO-A inhibitor, not MAO-B - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Moclobemide inhibits MAO-A (preferentially metabolizes serotonin, norepinephrine). Selegiline is MAO-B selective. Options A, B, C are correctly matched: fluoxetine is SSRI, mirtazapine is alpha-2 antagonist, venlafaxine is SNRI.
questions.keyConcept: Moclobemide selectively inhibits MAO-A; selegiline at low doses is MAO-B selective.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following drug interaction with TCA is wrong?
options: Alpha blocker / potential postural hypotensive effect
TCA / potentiate the effect of sympathomimitics
questions.explanation: SSRIs INCREASE TCA toxicity, not decrease - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. SSRIs inhibit CYP450 enzymes, increasing TCA levels and toxicity. Options A, B, D are correct: alpha blockers potentiate hypotension, TCAs potentiate sympathomimetics, MAOIs cause serotonin syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: SSRIs inhibit TCA metabolism via CYP450 inhibition, increasing TCA toxicity risk.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not adverse effect of Imipramine
options: Prolongation of QT interval leading to arrhythmia
Confusion, dry mouth and increase IOP
questions.explanation: Convulsion is NOT an imipramine adverse effect - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Imipramine (TCA) can cause seizures, especially in overdose. Options A, B, D are correct: QT prolongation, anticholinergic effects (confusion, dry mouth, increased IOP), insomnia and hallucinations are all TCA adverse effects.
questions.keyConcept: TCA overdose can cause seizures due to lowered seizure threshold and CNS toxicity.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following is not adverse effect encountered with fluoxetine?
questions.explanation: Sedation and dry mouth are NOT common with fluoxetine. Option D is incorrect. Fluoxetine causes activation (nausea, anxiety, insomnia), sexual dysfunction, and can increase suicide risk (especially in young patients). Sedation and dry mouth are characteristic of TCAs, not SSRIs.
questions.keyConcept: SSRIs like fluoxetine cause activating effects (nausea, insomnia, anxiety) rather than sedation.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following a do not induce sexual dysfunction
questions.explanation: Bupropion does NOT increase serotonin and has the least sexual dysfunction among antidepressants. Option D (bupropion alone) is correct as it does not induce sexual dysfunction.
questions.keyConcept: Bupropion's lack of serotonergic activity avoids sexual dysfunction common with other antidepressants.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following drug do not increase serotonin in the brain
questions.explanation: Bupropion does NOT increase serotonin in the brain. Option C is correct. Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) with no significant serotonin activity. Imipramine (A) is a TCA that blocks serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake. Fluoxetine (B) is an SSRI. Venlafaxine (D) is an SNRI. Mirtazapine (E) increases serotonin via alpha-2 blockade.
questions.keyConcept: Bupropion's mechanism involves dopamine and norepinephrine, not serotonin, distinguishing it from other antidepressants.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Fatal dermatitis is a serious adverse effect of which of the following drugs?
questions.explanation: Lamotrigine is associated with severe dermatologic reactions including Stevens‑Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which can be fatal. These risks are dose‑dependent and higher when combined with valproate.
questions.keyConcept: Lamotrigine carries a black box warning for serious skin reactions including Stevens‑Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following does not have an antidote?
questions.explanation: Thiopental is a barbiturate that lacks a specific antagonist; benzodiazepines can be reversed with flumazenil. This makes barbiturate overdose management more challenging.
questions.keyConcept: Barbiturates such as thiopental have no specific antidote, unlike benzodiazepines which have flumazenil.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following drugs is preferred in case of penicillin allergy in a patient with Streptococcus Pneumoniae?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is the preferred alternative for serious Streptococcus pneumoniae infections in penicillin‑allergic patients, covering multi‑drug resistant strains. Cefixime is a 3rd‑generation cephalosporin (cross‑reactivity risk), rifampicin is not monotherapy, and gentamicin lacks adequate pneumococcal coverage.
questions.keyConcept: Vancomycin is the standard alternative for serious pneumococcal infections in penicillin‑allergic patients.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following anti‑epileptic drug acts by binding to SV2A to modify glutamate release:
questions.explanation: Levetiracetam selectively binds to synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, modulating calcium‑dependent neurotransmitter release and exerting its antiepileptic effect.
questions.keyConcept: Levetiracetam's antiepileptic mechanism involves SV2A binding, which modulates vesicular neurotransmitter release.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Patient intolerant to SSRIs due to their correlation with sexual disturbances can instead take:
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine has lower rates of sexual dysfunction compared to SSRIs due to its unique alpha‑2 antagonism and 5‑HT2/5‑HT3 blocking properties, making it an alternative when sexual side effects are problematic.
questions.keyConcept: Mirtazapine has a favorable sexual side‑effect profile compared to SSRIs.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Moclobemide is preferred to phenelzine because:
options: It inhibits MAO‑A and MAO‑B enzymes
It is a selective MAO‑A inhibitor only
It can be safely used in combination with SSRIs
questions.explanation: Moclobemide is a reversible, selective MAO‑A inhibitor with fewer dietary restrictions compared to non‑selective, irreversible MAO inhibitors like phenelzine.
questions.keyConcept: Moclobemide's selectivity and reversibility for MAO‑A make it safer with fewer dietary interactions than phenelzine.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Gingival hygiene and care is highly recommended when taking which of the following drugs?
questions.explanation: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia in up to 50% of patients due to overgrowth of fibroblasts and collagen, necessitating rigorous oral hygiene and dental review.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin is notorious for causing gingival hyperplasia, requiring preventive dental care.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Flumazenil can be used as an antidote with which of the following drugs?
questions.explanation: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines by competitive antagonism at the GABA‑A receptor; it also antagonizes z‑zolpidem and zopiclone (Z‑drugs) which act via the same receptor.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil antagonizes benzodiazepines and Z‑drugs via competitive GABA‑A receptor blockade.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Lidocaine is preferred to bupivacaine in local anesthesia due to:
questions.explanation: Lidocaine has a lower pKa (~7.9) closer to physiological pH than bupivacaine (~8.1), resulting in a higher fraction of unionized drug and faster nerve penetration and onset.
questions.keyConcept: Lidocaine's lower pKa confers faster onset compared to bupivacaine in local anesthesia.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Chloramphenicol is the last antibiotic of choice to be used due to:
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol's most feared adverse effect is aplastic anemia, an idiosyncratic and potentially fatal bone marrow suppression, not anaphylactic shock.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol's most feared adverse effect is aplastic anemia, an idiosyncratic and potentially fatal bone marrow reaction.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Prophylaxis of close contact by rifampicin for 2 days is used in case of:
questions.explanation: Rifampicin 2-day prophylaxis is used for meningococcal contacts. None of the listed organisms (H. influenzae, S. agalactiae, S. pneumoniae) have this specific prophylaxis regimen.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin 2‑day prophylaxis is for meningococcal contacts, but none of the listed organisms match this indication.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Pseudocholelithiasis is associated with:
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone causes biliary pseudolithiasis (sludge) due to precipitation with calcium in the gallbladder, which is reversible upon discontinuation. It is not true gallstones.
questions.keyConcept: Ceftriaxone forms reversible biliary pseudolithiasis by precipitating with calcium in bile.

questions.subject: pharma
